docs.title: AWS Cloud overview: Global Infrastructure, Regions and Availability Zones, Edge Locations and CloudFront
Definition
docs.text:
Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of IT resources (compute, storage, networking, databases and higher-level services) over the Internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of buying and operating physical servers, an organisation provisions resources programmatically from a provider that runs the physical infrastructure at massive scale.

The key mental shift: stop thinking of infrastructure as hardware and start thinking of it as software.

Physical Server Example

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
docs.text:
Before cloud computing, running a production application meant:

  1. Capital expenditure (CapEx). Buying servers, storage, network gear, power and cooling, often 6 to 12 months before the first user.
  2. Capacity guessing. Forecasting peak demand years ahead. Over-provisioning wasted money; under-provisioning caused outages at the moment of success.
  3. Single points of failure. Most companies had one data centre. A fire, flood or fibre cut took the business offline.
  4. Undifferentiated heavy lifting. Engineers racked servers and replaced disks instead of building features.
  5. Unaffordable global reach. Low latency on every continent required data centres on every continent.

AWS inverts each problem:

Traditional approach AWS approach Benefit Buy hardware up front (CapEx) Rent capacity per second/hour (OpEx) No upfront investment; cost tracks usage Forecast capacity years ahead Elastic scaling on demand Capacity matches actual load One data centre, one fault domain Multiple AZs per Region, multiple Regions Engineered fault isolation Build your own global footprint 30+ Regions, 100+ AZs, 700+ PoPs already built Global deployment in minutes Operate power, cooling, physical security AWS operates the facility layer Teams focus on applications

docs.title: Cloud Service Models
docs.text:
Cloud Service Model

Each service model is a different split of responsibility. Moving down the table, you manage less and control less.

Model You manage Provider manages AWS examples IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) OS, runtime, application, data Hardware, virtualisation, network Amazon EC2, Amazon VPC, Amazon EBS PaaS (Platform as a Service) Application and data Everything below the application, including the OS AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Amazon RDS FaaS (Function as a Service) Function code and its configuration Servers, OS, runtime, scaling AWS Lambda SaaS (Software as a Service) Only how you use the product The entire application Web-based email, Amazon WorkMail
  • IaaS gives the most flexibility and control and is closest to traditional IT.
  • PaaS removes the need to manage hardware and operating systems so you focus on deploying applications.
  • FaaS (often called serverless) goes further: you deploy individual functions that run only when triggered. See 1.3 AWS Compute Services.
  • SaaS is a finished product; you think only about using it.

The trade-off is control versus operational effort

No model is "better". IaaS suits workloads that need OS-level control; managed models suit teams that want to spend their time on application code. Cloud-native designs in this module lean towards managed services.

docs.title: Cloud Deployment Models
docs.text:
Cloud Deployment Model Model What it means Typical reason Cloud All parts of the application run in the cloud, either built there or migrated Gain full elasticity and managed services Hybrid Cloud resources connected to existing on-premises systems Extend into the cloud gradually while keeping internal systems On-premises (private cloud) Resources in your own data centre using virtualisation and management tools Dedicated resources or a hard requirement to stay on-site

On-premises deployment does not provide most cloud benefits; it is often legacy infrastructure with better tooling. See What is cloud computing? for more.

docs.title: What is AWS?
docs.text:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a secure cloud platform offering a broad set of global, on-demand services: compute, storage, networking, databases and the tools to manage them. Resources are ready in minutes, can be scaled up or down automatically, and are billed as an operational expense.

AWS services are designed as building blocks: you assemble them into a solution and change the assembly as needs change.

AWS Stats

  • $128.7 billion in annual revenue as of 2025
  • About 31% of the global cloud market, making AWS the largest provider
  • 15 consecutive years as market leader
  • More than 1 million active customers worldwide

docs.title: AWS Global Infrastructure
docs.text:
The AWS Global Infrastructure is the physical foundation on which every AWS service runs. It has three layers:

Layer What it is Primary purpose Region A geographic area containing multiple isolated data-centre clusters Data residency, service hosting, geographic fault isolation Availability Zone (AZ) One or more discrete data centres in a Region, with independent power, cooling and networking Fault isolation within a Region; the building block of high availability Edge Location / Point of Presence (PoP) A small facility close to end users Low-latency content delivery (CloudFront), DNS resolution (Route 53), DDoS absorption 3 layers of Global Infrastructure

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Every resource you create lives somewhere physically. Choosing the right "where" is one of the first decisions in any cloud design.

Fault domains and latency domains

Regions, AZs and Edge Locations are not trivia to memorise. They are fault domains and latency domains. Every availability, disaster-recovery, latency and compliance decision on AWS is a decision about how to place workloads across these three layers.

docs.title: Why this structure?
docs.text:
AWS could have offered one flat pool of "servers somewhere". It did not, for three reasons:

Reason Problem How the structure solves it Physics Light in fibre adds about 5 microseconds per km; Sydney to Virginia is about 200 ms round trip however fast the server is Proximity: Regions on every continent, Edge Locations in hundreds of cities Failure correlation Servers in one building share power and cooling; buildings in one city share floods and grid failures AZs contain local disasters; Regions contain large-scale ones Law GDPR and data-sovereignty laws require data to stay in a jurisdiction Regions are an explicit, auditable data boundary

docs.title: Region
docs.text:
A Region is a geographic location where AWS clusters data centres, for example us-east-1 (N. Virginia), eu-west-1 (Ireland), ap-southeast-1 (Singapore).

  • Each Region has multiple AZs (at least three for modern Regions).
  • Regions are isolated: a failure in one is designed not to affect any other.
  • Data does not leave a Region unless you explicitly replicate or move it. This is the foundation of data-residency compliance.
  • Each Region has its own service control planes, so an API outage in one Region does not block management in another.
  • Not every service or instance type exists in every Region. New services usually launch in large Regions first, and smaller Regions can cost more. China and GovCloud Regions require separate accounts.

docs.title: Availability Zone (AZ)
docs.text:
An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centres with redundant power, networking and connectivity, in separate facilities within a Region.

  • AZs are physically separated (typically kilometres to roughly 100 km apart): far enough to avoid sharing most disasters, close enough for synchronous replication (round trip generally under 1 to 2 ms).
  • Each AZ has independent power, cooling and physical security, linked to the other AZs by redundant private fibre.
  • AZs are named by appending a letter to the Region code: us-east-1a, us-east-1b.

AZ names are randomised per account

The mapping from an AZ name (us-east-1a) to a physical zone is shuffled independently for each account, to spread load evenly. Your us-east-1a is probably not another account's us-east-1a. When zones must be coordinated across accounts, use the AZ ID (such as use1-az4), which is the same for everyone.

docs.title: Fault domain and blast radius
docs.text:
A fault domain is a set of resources that share a failure mode: a rack (shared switch), a data centre (shared power), an AZ, a Region. Blast radius is the scope of impact when something fails.

AWS architecture in one sentence: place redundant resources in different fault domains so that any single failure has a bounded blast radius.

Fault domain and Blast Radius

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

docs.title: High Availability vs Fault Tolerance vs Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
Concept Definition Typical AWS mechanism High Availability (HA) The system stays operational despite component failure, possibly with brief degradation Multi-AZ deployment behind a load balancer; RDS Multi-AZ failover Fault Tolerance The system keeps operating with no user-visible interruption Active-active redundancy across AZs; S3 replicating every object across at least 3 AZs Disaster Recovery (DR) Recovering service in a different location after a large-scale event Multi-Region: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active

Two metrics drive DR design:

  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long recovery may take.
  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data loss is tolerable.

The DR strategies form a ladder: backup and restore (hours of RTO, cheapest) → pilot light (data replicated, minimal compute) → warm standby (scaled-down full stack) → active-active (full stack in two Regions, most expensive). Choose by RTO/RPO and pay accordingly.

Durability is not availability

Durability means data is not lost; availability means data is reachable. S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability through multi-AZ replication. A single EBS volume lives in one AZ and needs snapshots for durability beyond it. See 6.1 AWS Storage Solutions.

docs.title: Edge Locations and Amazon CloudFront
docs.text:
An Edge Location is a small AWS facility in a major city, often inside an Internet exchange point. It hosts edge services: CloudFront caches, Route 53 DNS servers, AWS Shield DDoS protection, AWS WAF and Global Accelerator entry points. There are far more Edge Locations than Regions, because their job is proximity.

Property Region / AZ Edge Location Can you launch EC2 or RDS there? Yes No Purpose Run applications and store data Cache content, terminate connections, resolve DNS Scale 30+ Regions / 100+ AZs 700+ PoPs in 100+ cities Services Nearly all CloudFront, Route 53, Shield, WAF, Global Accelerator, edge functions

Amazon CloudFront is AWS's Content Delivery Network (CDN). A CDN caches copies of content near users, giving two wins:

  1. Proximity. A cache hit is served from tens of kilometres away, not thousands.
  2. Offload. The origin serves each object once per cache lifetime, not once per user.

Key CloudFront terms:

Term Meaning Distribution A CloudFront configuration: origins, behaviours and settings Origin Where the real content lives: an S3 bucket, an ALB, API Gateway or any HTTP server TTL How long an object may be served from cache before it is checked again Cache hit ratio Fraction of requests served from cache; the main efficiency measure Regional Edge Cache A larger mid-tier cache between Edge Locations and the origin; an edge miss checks it before going to the origin Invalidation Removing objects from caches before their TTL expires CloudFront cache decision (per request)

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Even uncached, dynamic requests benefit: CloudFront terminates TLS near the user and carries traffic to the origin over the AWS private backbone instead of the public Internet.

CloudFront vs Global Accelerator

Both use the edge network. CloudFront is an HTTP cache. Global Accelerator gives static anycast IP addresses and routes TCP/UDP traffic over the backbone with no caching, which suits non-HTTP workloads such as game servers.

DNS is how users find the edge: Route 53 resolves your domain to the CloudFront distribution. Route 53 itself, including routing policies and health checks, is covered in 1.6 AWS Network Services.

docs.title: Extensions of the Region model
docs.text: Extension What it is Use case Local Zones Single-zone extensions of a Region in additional metros (for example, Los Angeles for us-west-2) Single-digit-millisecond latency to users in that city Wavelength Zones AWS infrastructure embedded in 5G telecom networks Ultra-low latency for mobile devices AWS Outposts AWS-managed racks installed in your data centre Workloads that must stay on-site but want AWS APIs GovCloud / sovereign Regions Regions with extra legal and personnel restrictions Government and regulated workloads

docs.title: Global, Regional and Zonal services
docs.text:
Scope Examples Implication Global IAM, Route 53, CloudFront One logical instance for the whole account; no Region choice Regional S3 buckets, DynamoDB, SQS, Lambda, VPC, ALB You choose the Region; the service spans multiple AZs internally Zonal EC2 instances, EBS volumes, subnets Bound to one AZ; you are responsible for multi-AZ redundancy

Architect's rule of thumb

Regional managed services (S3, DynamoDB, SQS, Lambda) give you multi-AZ resilience automatically. Zonal building blocks (EC2, EBS) make multi-AZ your job. This is one of the strongest arguments for managed, cloud-native architectures, and it recurs throughout DSO303.

Global name, Regional home

S3 bucket names are globally unique, but each bucket lives in one Region.

docs.title: How the Layers Fit Together
docs.text:
A typical production web request passes through all three layers:

Step Component Layer Role 1 Route 53 Edge (global) Resolves the domain to CloudFront 2 CloudFront + WAF + Shield Edge (global) Terminates TLS, serves cached content, filters attacks 3 Application Load Balancer Regional, multi-AZ Spreads requests across healthy targets in several AZs 4 Compute (EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda) Zonal or Regional Runs the application 5 S3, RDS, DynamoDB Regional Stores data, replicated across AZs

The services in steps 3 to 5 are introduced in 1.3, 1.4, 1.5 and 1.6.

Architectural Components of Global Infra

Image Source: AI Generated (ChatGPT)

Example: Integrating Different Services

docs.title: Choosing a Region
docs.text:
Criteria, in the order most organisations apply them:

  1. Compliance and data residency. A legal constraint overrides everything else.
  2. Latency to users. Pick the Region closest to your users; measure, do not assume.
  3. Service availability. Confirm every service and instance type you need exists there.
  4. Cost. Identical resources can differ noticeably in price between Regions.
  5. Sustainability and proximity to partners or on-premises sites.
Region Selection Work Flow

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

docs.title: Using AZs
docs.text:
• VPC subnets are created per AZ. Load balancers, Auto Scaling groups, ECS services and EKS node groups take a list of subnets: that list is your AZ spread.
  • Use at least two AZs for HA; three is preferred. Losing one of three AZs removes only about a third of capacity and leaves a majority for clustered systems.
  • Availability is limited by the weakest link. A multi-AZ application tied to a single-AZ database inherits the database's availability.
  • Design for static stability: run enough spare capacity in every AZ that a failure needs no new launches or control-plane actions to recover.

docs.title: Latency anchors
docs.text:
Path Typical latency Within one AZ Under 1 ms Between AZs in a Region About 1 to 2 ms User to nearest Edge Location About 5 to 30 ms Between Regions / user to a remote Region Tens to hundreds of ms

These numbers explain why synchronous replication stops at the Region boundary, and why CloudFront exists.

docs.title: Single-AZ, multi-AZ or multi-Region?
docs.text:
Option When to use Cost of the choice Single-AZ Development and test only One AZ event takes the system down Multi-AZ The production default Small cross-AZ data-transfer charges Multi-Region Only when RTO/RPO, global latency or regulation demands it Can double infrastructure cost; multiplies pipelines, monitoring and data-consistency questions

The single-AZ production system

Running production in one AZ to avoid cross-AZ transfer charges is a classic false economy. AZ-level events happen every year somewhere. Multi-AZ is the non-negotiable production baseline in this module.

docs.title: Operating It: Security, Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Security

  • Treat Regions as compliance boundaries. Organisations can block resource creation outside approved Regions using the aws:RequestedRegion condition key in a Service Control Policy (see 8.1).
  • KMS keys are Regional: data encrypted in one Region needs a key strategy to be readable in another (see 8.3).
  • The ACM certificate used by CloudFront must be requested in us-east-1.
  • Edge services absorb attacks before they reach your Region: Shield Standard is automatic and free on CloudFront and Route 53; WAF filters web attacks at the edge (see 8.2).
  • Keep origins private: with Origin Access Control (OAC), an S3 bucket stays private while CloudFront serves it globally.

Performance

  • Serve users from the edge; choose Regions by measured latency.
  • Use versioned file names (app.3f9a1c.js) with long TTLs instead of frequent invalidations.
  • Put in the cache key only what changes the response. Forwarding all cookies or query strings fragments the cache and destroys the hit ratio.

Cost: placement drives the bill

Traffic Billed? Data transfer in from the Internet Free Data transfer out to the Internet Billed per GB Between AZs Billed (about $0.01/GB each direction) Between Regions Billed at higher rates From AWS origins (S3, ALB) to CloudFront Free

Because origin fetches are free, a high cache hit ratio can make CloudFront cheaper than serving directly from the Region while also being faster. Chatty microservices spread across AZs pay cross-AZ charges constantly. Use price classes to exclude expensive edge geographies if your users are local.

Monitoring

  • Global services such as CloudFront publish CloudWatch metrics to us-east-1.
  • Compare metrics per AZ: one AZ diverging from the others is the classic early sign of a zonal problem. Averages hide it.
  • Enable CloudTrail in all Regions to catch activity in Regions you do not use.
  • The AWS Health Dashboard shows when a Region, AZ or edge service is impaired. Observability in depth is covered in Unit 7.

docs.title: Industry Use Cases
docs.text: Sector Use of Regions, AZs and the edge Media and streaming Nearly all bytes delivered from edge caches; live-event spikes absorbed at the edge E-commerce Multi-AZ storefronts; CloudFront for catalogue images; Route 53 failover Banking and fintech In-country Region for residency; Multi-AZ databases; warm-standby second Region for regulator-mandated DR Gaming Regions per continent for game servers; Global Accelerator for UDP; CloudFront for large patch downloads Government GovCloud and sovereign Regions; strict Region allowlists Healthcare Residency-driven Region choice; Multi-AZ patient-record systems IoT and automotive Regional analytics; Wavelength for vehicle-to-cloud latency

docs.title: Advantages and Limitations
docs.text: Advantages Limitations Engineered fault isolation: HA becomes a configuration choice (a list of subnets), not a construction project The speed of light is fixed: multi-Region synchronous consistency is impractical, so multi-Region data accepts either replication lag (RPO above zero) or slow writes Global reach in minutes with the same template in any Region Regions are not equal: services, instance types and prices vary; a Region choice is hard to reverse once data accumulates Elasticity without a capacity gamble Cross-boundary traffic costs money: resilience has a per-gigabyte price Compliance as configuration: Region choice plus enforcement, with an audit trail Quotas are Regional: a DR Region with default quotas can fail exactly when needed Latency solved at two scales: Regions for continents, the edge for the last mile Caching adds consistency problems: stale content, invalidation cost, personalised content caches poorly Attacks absorbed at the edge before they reach your Regional resources Operational multiplication: each extra Region multiplies pipelines, dashboards and on-call load

docs.title: Beginner Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it is wrong Do instead Deploying everything into one AZ or subnet One AZ event takes everything down Spread across at least two, ideally three AZs Assuming us-east-1a is the same zone in every account AZ names are shuffled per account Use AZ IDs across accounts "CloudFront caches content in AZs" Caches live in Edge Locations, not AZs Keep the three layers distinct Believing data replicates between Regions automatically It never does without explicit configuration Configure cross-Region replication deliberately Hard-coding a Region in code or templates Blocks multi-Region deployment later Make the Region a parameter Making an S3 bucket public "so CloudFront works" Exposes the data directly Use Origin Access Control Requesting the CloudFront certificate in the wrong Region CloudFront only uses ACM certificates from us-east-1 Request it in us-east-1

docs.title: Production Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Remedy Multi-AZ compute with a single-AZ database or single NAT gateway Hidden zonal single point of failure Make every tier multi-AZ Forwarding all cookies and headers to the origin Hit ratio collapses; "CloudFront does not help" Minimal cache key Recovery that depends on launching new resources Fails when the control plane is impaired Static stability: spare capacity already running Never testing AZ or Region failover DR exists only in a diagram Regular failure drills Leaving default quotas in the DR Region Failover cannot scale Raise quotas in advance

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The AWS global infrastructure is a three-layer answer to three permanent problems: Regions answer law and geography, Availability Zones answer failure, and Edge Locations with CloudFront answer the speed of light.

Area Key lesson Service and deployment models IaaS → PaaS → FaaS → SaaS trades control for less operational work; cloud, hybrid and on-premises describe where it runs Regions Isolated geographic areas; data stays in a Region unless you move it; choose by compliance, latency, services, cost Availability Zones Separate data centres close enough for synchronous replication; multi-AZ is the production baseline Edge and CloudFront Edge Locations cache and terminate connections near users; they cannot run EC2 HA, fault tolerance, DR HA survives with brief degradation, fault tolerance with none; DR recovers elsewhere, sized by RTO and RPO Service scope Global, Regional and Zonal; Regional managed services give multi-AZ for free, Zonal ones make it your job Cost Placement drives cost: egress, cross-AZ and cross-Region traffic are billed; CloudFront can reduce egress cost

Next: with the physical foundation in place, 1.2 AWS IAM explains who is allowed to do what on it.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: What Is IAM?
docs.text:
IAM Identity and Access Management is the AWS service that answers exactly two questions for every single request that ever reaches AWS:

1. WHO are you?            →  Authentication
2. Are you ALLOWED to do   →  Authorization
   this specific action
   on this specific
   resource?

Every other AWS service depends on it. When you run aws s3 ls, AWS does not simply list your buckets it first identifies you, then asks IAM whether you are permitted to call s3:ListAllMyBuckets. If IAM says no, you get AccessDenied and nothing else happens.

docs.title: Why IAM Exists
docs.text:
Before cloud, security was mostly physical and network based: the server was in a locked room behind a firewall. In the cloud there is no locked room. The only thing standing between your company's data and the internet is an identity and a policy document.

IAM exists so that you can express, precisely and in machine-readable form, statements such as:

  • "The reporting application may read student transcripts but may never delete them."
  • "Developers may start and stop test servers, but only in the Singapore region."
  • "This virtual machine may write to this one storage bucket, and nothing else."

docs.title: Where IAM Is Used in Real Systems
docs.text:
Real-world situation IAM feature that solves it A new engineer joins the team A user in the corporate identity provider, signed in through IAM Identity Center (in a single small account, an IAM user added to an IAM group) A CI/CD pipeline deploys code An IAM role assumed by the pipeline A server needs to read a storage bucket An IAM role attached to the server via an instance profile An auditor needs read-only access to everything An AWS managed policy (ReadOnlyAccess) A contractor must only touch one project's resources A customer managed policy scoped by resource ARN Temporary 1-hour access for an emergency STS temporary credentials

See 8.1 AWS Identity and Access Management for the full treatment of identities, policies and policy evaluation, STS, and AWS Organizations.

docs.title: Compute Services on AWS  EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda and Fargate
Definition
docs.text:
Compute services run your application code. They provide CPU, memory and an execution context for a process. Storage services hold data at rest, networking services move it, and compute services transform it.

AWS Compute Services

AWS offers compute at several levels of abstraction. The higher the abstraction, the more of the stack AWS manages, and the less control you keep.

Service Model Unit of deployment AWS manages You manage Amazon EC2 Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) Virtual machine instance Hosts, hypervisor, network, hardware failure Guest OS, patching, runtime, application, scaling, capacity Amazon ECS on EC2 Containers as a Service Task (one or more containers) Orchestration control plane, scheduling Container image, EC2 host fleet, host patching, capacity ECS or EKS on Fargate Serverless containers Task or Pod Everything below the container: host, OS, agent, capacity Container image, task sizing, IAM, network settings Amazon EKS Managed Kubernetes Pod Kubernetes control plane, etcd, control plane upgrades Worker nodes (or Fargate profiles), add-ons, manifests, upgrades AWS Lambda Function as a Service (FaaS) Function invocation Everything except your code and configuration Handler code, memory, IAM role, event sources

The key idea of this topic

You are not choosing the "best" or "most modern" service. You are choosing how much of the operational stack you want to own, and accepting the constraints that come with handing the rest to AWS.

docs.title: The compute spectrum
docs.text:
Level of Control in AWS

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Moving from EC2 towards Lambda:

  • Operational burden falls. First you stop patching kernels, then you stop managing hosts, then you stop thinking about servers.
  • Billing gets finer. Per-second instances, then per-second tasks, then per-millisecond invocations.
  • Constraints tighten. Lambda has a maximum duration, a package size limit and a stateless model. EC2 has none of these.
  • Portability changes. Container images run on any cloud. Lambda business logic ports, but its event wiring does not.

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
The problem before cloud compute
docs.text: Traditional data centre AWS compute Capacity bought before demand was known; utilisation often 10–20 percent Pay for what you use; scale with real demand Provisioning took weeks Seconds to minutes through an API Capital expenditure, approval for every experiment Operating expenditure; terminate when finished Manual configuration and hardware repair Automatic replacement by an Auto Scaling group No way to scale down: you cannot un-buy a server Scale in as easily as out

docs.title: How AWS compute evolved
docs.text:
Each service solved a problem the previous one left open.

Service (year) Problem it solved What it left open EC2 (2006) Virtual machines through an API in minutes, pay as you go. Made elasticity possible You still patch an OS and deploy onto each machine Containers Packaging: one immutable image runs the same everywhere Placement: which host runs which container, and what happens when a host dies ECS (2014) AWS-native orchestration, integrated with IAM, ELB and CloudWatch You still run the EC2 hosts Lambda (2014) Run a function on demand, scale from zero, pay per millisecond Short, stateless work only Fargate (2017) Containers with no EC2 instances to manage Higher unit price; fewer host features EKS (2018) Managed Kubernetes, the open-source standard, for portability and ecosystem Kubernetes complexity

The evolution is additive, not a replacement

Lambda did not replace EC2, and EKS did not replace ECS. Mature AWS estates run all of them, each for the workload it fits: EC2 for a licensed legacy database, Kubernetes for a microservice platform, Lambda for event glue.

docs.title: Virtualisation and multi-tenancy
docs.text:
A hypervisor partitions one physical server into isolated virtual machines (VMs). Each VM believes it has its own CPU, memory, disks and network. The hypervisor stops one tenant reading another's memory. On AWS, the Nitro System moves most of this work onto dedicated hardware.

Types of Hypervisor

Multi-tenancy means many customers share physical hardware. It is what makes cloud economics work. EC2 tenancy is shared by default; Dedicated Instances keep your hardware free of other accounts, and Dedicated Hosts give you a specific physical server with visible sockets and cores, which matters for per-socket licensing.

docs.title: Containers versus virtual machines
docs.text:
Virtual machine model VS Container Model

A container isolates a process at the operating-system level. It has no kernel of its own. Linux namespaces give it its own view of processes, network and filesystem; cgroups limit its CPU and memory.

Property Virtual machine Container Isolation boundary Separate kernel, hardware-virtualised Shared kernel, namespaces Start time Tens of seconds to minutes Milliseconds to seconds Image size Gigabytes Tens to hundreds of megabytes Density per host Tens Hundreds Isolation strength Very strong Strong, but the shared kernel is a shared attack surface Typical use Full OS environments, legacy software Microservices, stateless processes

A container is not as strong a boundary as a VM

A kernel vulnerability can, in principle, allow container escape. This is why Fargate and Lambda place each task or execution environment in its own lightweight VM (a Firecracker microVM) rather than sharing a kernel between customers.

A container image is immutable: the image tested in staging is exactly the image running in production, and rollback means redeploying an earlier tag. Images are stored in Amazon ECR. Images, Dockerfiles and ECR are covered in 2.1 Docker and Amazon ECR.

docs.title: Orchestration
docs.text:
Orchestration is the automated management of containers across a fleet of hosts. An orchestrator:

  • schedules containers onto hosts with enough CPU and memory;
  • reconciles actual state with desired state, replacing failed containers;
  • registers containers with load balancers and service discovery;
  • rolls out new versions without downtime.

The model is declarative. You do not say "start three containers"; you declare "desired count is three", and a control loop keeps it true, even after failures you never see.

Modern Container Orchestration

docs.title: Serverless
docs.text:
Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means four things are true at once:

  1. You do not provision or manage servers.
  2. Scaling is automatic, including scaling to zero.
  3. You pay for use, with no charge when idle.
  4. Availability across Availability Zones (AZs) is built in.

Lambda meets all four. Fargate meets the first, the fourth and most of the second, but an idle Fargate task still bills. That is why Fargate is called "serverless containers" rather than fully serverless.

docs.title: Statelessness
docs.text:
A stateless compute node holds nothing that would matter if it were lost. Sessions, uploads and caches live in external services such as DynamoDB, ElastiCache, S3 or RDS (1.4, 1.5).

Statelessness is what makes elasticity possible. If any instance can be terminated at any moment without data loss, the platform is free to replace instances for scaling, patching, Spot reclamation or failure recovery.

The classic statefulness bug

A team keeps user sessions in each EC2 instance's memory and enables sticky sessions on the load balancer. It works until an instance is replaced during a deployment, and those users are logged out mid-checkout. The fix is not more stickiness; it is moving session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB.

docs.title: Scalability, elasticity and availability
docs.text:
These terms are often confused.

Term Meaning Mechanism on AWS Scalability Handling more load by adding resources More instances, tasks, Pods or concurrent executions Elasticity Scaling out and back in automatically with demand Auto Scaling groups, ECS service auto scaling, Kubernetes HPA, Lambda concurrency High availability Continuing to operate when a component fails Multi-AZ deployment, health checks, redundancy Fault tolerance Continuing with no degradation when a component fails Spare capacity (N+1), retries, idempotency

Vertical scaling (a bigger instance) has a ceiling and needs a restart. Horizontal scaling (more instances) is the cloud-native default. Use vertical scaling only where work cannot be split, such as a single-writer relational database.

docs.title: Shared responsibility for compute
docs.text:
AWS is responsible for security of the cloud; you are responsible for security in the cloud. Where the line falls is exactly what separates the compute services.

graph TD
    subgraph EC2["Amazon EC2"]
        E1["Customer: App, Runtime, Guest OS, Patching, Firewall Rules"]
        E2["AWS: Hypervisor, Hardware, Network, Facilities"]
    end
    subgraph FG["ECS or EKS on Fargate"]
        F1["Customer: App, Container Image, Task IAM, Networking Config"]
        F2["AWS: Host OS, Agent, Capacity, Hypervisor, Hardware"]
    end
    subgraph LM["AWS Lambda"]
        L1["Customer: Function Code, Memory Config, IAM Role"]
        L2["AWS: Runtime, Execution Environment, Scaling, Everything Else"]
    end

docs.title: AWS Service Deep Dive
docs.text:
On numbers and quotas

Many limits below are soft quotas that can be raised through Service Quotas, and some vary by Region. Treat them as design signals and check the current documentation and the AWS Pricing Calculator before committing to a design.

docs.title: Amazon EC2
docs.text: EC2 provides resizable virtual machines with full control of the operating system. Anything that runs on a physical server can run on EC2: legacy software, licensed products, custom kernels, GPU workloads.

docs.title: What an instance is made of
docs.text:
An instance is launched from an AMI (Amazon Machine Image: the root volume template) with an instance type (a fixed vCPU, memory and network combination, for example m7g.large). It connects to a subnet through an ENI with security groups, stores data on persistent EBS volumes or fast but temporary instance store disks (lost on stop or termination), receives an IAM role through an instance profile, and can run a user data script at first boot.

Instance families. Match the hardware to the workload rather than over-buying one dimension.

Family Letters Optimised for Example workload General purpose M, T Balanced CPU and memory Web servers, small databases Compute optimised C High CPU per GB Batch processing, encoding, game servers Memory optimised R, X High memory per vCPU Databases, in-memory caches Storage optimised I, D Fast local disk High-I/O databases, data warehousing Accelerated P, G, Inf, Trn GPUs and ML chips Machine learning, graphics

A g in the name (for example m7g) means Graviton, AWS's ARM processor. It usually gives better price-performance but needs arm64 builds. T instances use CPU credits: sustained load exhausts them and the instance is throttled to its baseline, a classic cause of "it worked in testing" latency.

docs.title: Purchasing options
docs.text:
Option How it works Best for On-Demand Pay per second, no commitment Unpredictable load, development, spikes Savings Plans Commit to a dollar-per-hour spend for one or three years; discounts commonly 30–70 percent. Compute Savings Plans also cover Fargate and Lambda Steady baseline load Reserved Instances Commit to a specific instance configuration for one or three years Long-lived, unchanging workloads Spot Instances Spare capacity at discounts often 70–90 percent; reclaimed with a two-minute notice Fault-tolerant, interruptible work: batch, CI runners Dedicated Hosts / Instances Hardware isolation Regulation or per-socket licensing Capacity Reservations Reserve capacity in one AZ, no term commitment A known event or disaster recovery

Auto Scaling basics. An Auto Scaling group (ASG) keeps a desired number of instances running across AZs, replaces unhealthy ones, and scales using a launch template.

  • Target tracking keeps a metric at a target, like a thermostat (for example, 50 percent average CPU).
  • Scheduled and predictive scaling handle known daily patterns.
  • The warm-up period excludes booting instances from metrics; the cooldown prevents oscillation.
  • Set the health check type to ELB so an instance failing the application health check is replaced, not just one failing EC2 status checks.

Availability. An instance lives in one AZ. Availability comes from an ASG across several AZs behind a load balancer (1.6).

When EC2 is the right answer

Choose EC2 when you need OS-level control, host-licensed software, a custom kernel, GPUs, or long-running steady load that suits Savings Plans, or when you are lifting and shifting an existing application before modernising it.

docs.title: Amazon ECS
docs.text:
Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) is AWS's own container orchestrator. Its control plane is fully managed and has no charge; you pay only for the capacity your tasks use.

A task definition is a versioned blueprint (images, CPU and memory, ports, secrets, IAM roles). A task is a running copy of it. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running behind a load balancer. A cluster groups services and capacity, and a capacity provider says where tasks run: an Auto Scaling group, FARGATE or FARGATE_SPOT.

Two points to remember now:

  • Two IAM roles per task. The task execution role lets ECS pull images, write logs and fetch secrets. The task role is what your application code uses.
  • Two scaling layers on EC2, one on Fargate. Service auto scaling changes the task count; on EC2 capacity, the instance count must scale as well.

Full treatment: 2.2 Amazon ECS (clusters, networking, IAM roles) and 2.3 Container Orchestration with Amazon ECS (placement, scaling, deployments).

docs.title: Amazon EKS
docs.text:
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) runs standard Kubernetes on AWS. AWS operates the control plane (API server and etcd) across at least three AZs; you choose the data plane: managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Fargate profiles, Karpenter or EKS Auto Mode.

  • Pricing. An hourly fee per cluster, plus the EC2 or Fargate capacity you use. ECS has no such fee.
  • Upgrades are mandatory and recurring. Each Kubernetes version has a limited standard support window; extended support costs more.
  • Three scaling layers. Pods horizontally (HPA), Pods vertically (VPA), and nodes (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter).
  • Why choose it. The Kubernetes ecosystem (Helm, operators, service meshes) and portability across clouds.

Full treatment: 3.1 Amazon EKS Architecture, 3.2 Deploying Applications on Amazon EKS and 3.3 Amazon EKS Advanced Concepts.

docs.title: AWS Lambda
docs.text:
Lambda runs code in response to events, with no servers or capacity to manage. It scales automatically from zero and charges only for the time your code runs.

A function is your code (a ZIP package, or a container image up to 10 GB), a runtime (managed Node.js, Python, Java, .NET or Ruby, or a custom runtime), a handler entry point, a memory setting from 128 MB to 10,240 MB (CPU is allocated in proportion to memory), a timeout of up to 15 minutes, and an execution role. Layers, environment variables, VPC attachment and /tmp storage (512 MB to 10,240 MB) are optional.

How invocation works. Each request runs in an execution environment (a Firecracker microVM) that handles one request at a time. If a warm environment is free, the request reuses it. If not, Lambda creates a new one: a cold start, which must load the code and run initialisation before the handler. Cold starts range from about 100–300 ms for a small interpreted function to several seconds for large JVM or .NET applications.

docs.title: Important features
docs.text: Feature Purpose Versions and aliases Immutable versions; aliases point to them and can split traffic for canary releases Reserved concurrency Caps and guarantees a function's concurrency; protects other functions and downstream databases. Setting it to zero is an emergency stop Provisioned concurrency Pre-warms environments to remove cold starts, at extra cost SnapStart Restores a snapshot of an initialised environment to cut cold starts (for example, Java) Event source mappings Lambda polls SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams and invokes the function with batches Destinations and DLQs Route failed asynchronous events somewhere visible instead of losing them

docs.title: Limits that decide whether Lambda fits
docs.text:
Limit Value Design implication Maximum duration 15 minutes (hard) Longer jobs go to Fargate, AWS Batch or Step Functions Memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB About one vCPU near 1,769 MB, up to about six at maximum Package size 50 MB zipped upload, 250 MB unzipped with layers, 10 GB as an image Large models need the image path or EFS Payload 6 MB synchronous, 256 KB asynchronous (hard) Store large data in S3 and pass a reference Concurrency 1,000 per account per Region by default (soft) Raise it before a launch; it is shared by all functions Environment variables 4 KB total Larger configuration goes in Parameter Store or Secrets Manager State No guaranteed environment reuse Never rely on memory surviving between invocations

Pricing. You pay for requests and GB-seconds (memory multiplied by duration), plus provisioned concurrency if used. arm64 is cheaper per GB-second. Watch the surrounding costs: API Gateway requests, CloudWatch Logs, and NAT for VPC-attached functions.

More memory can cost less

Because CPU grows with memory, a function taking 2,000 ms at 512 MB may take 400 ms at 1,536 MB. Fewer GB-seconds are used even though the rate per millisecond is higher. Measure with AWS Lambda Power Tuning rather than guessing.

Scaling and availability. Concurrency equals the number of environments running at once. Lambda adds environments in bursts, far faster than an ASG adds instances. Under load, latency per request stays flat; concurrency rises instead. Lambda runs across multiple AZs automatically; if you attach it to a VPC, give it subnets in several AZs.

docs.title: AWS Fargate as a Capacity Mode
docs.text:
Fargate is often mistaken for a fourth orchestrator. It is not. Fargate is a way of supplying capacity to ECS or EKS; you still need one of those orchestrators. See 2.2 Amazon ECS for the ECS launch-type decision and 3.3 Amazon EKS Advanced Concepts for Fargate on EKS.

Aspect ECS or EKS on EC2 ECS or EKS on Fargate Host management Yours AWS Billing Per instance-second, whether full or not Per requested vCPU and GB, per second DaemonSets, host agents, privileged containers Supported Not supported GPUs Supported Not supported Spot EC2 Spot Fargate Spot on ECS; not available on EKS Fargate Cheaper when Utilisation is high and steady Utilisation is low or spiky

The Fargate cost heuristic

Fargate's per-vCPU rate is higher than EC2's, but you pay only for what tasks request. Fargate tends to win when instances would sit below roughly 60–70 percent utilisation; well-packed EC2 with Savings Plans or Spot wins above that. Include the engineering time spent patching and scaling nodes: for most teams it outweighs the raw price difference.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text:
Compute is never deployed alone. The components below appear in nearly every design in this module.

Component Role around compute Covered in Route 53, CloudFront DNS and edge caching in front of compute 1.6 Application / Network Load Balancer Spread traffic across instances, tasks or Pods; health checks 1.6 API Gateway API front door, especially for Lambda 4.2 VPC, subnets, security groups Network isolation; compute belongs in private subnets 1.6, 8.2 Auto Scaling group Keeps EC2 capacity at the desired count This topic ECR Stores container images 2.1 IAM roles Temporary credentials for every compute service 8.1 S3, EBS, EFS, RDS, DynamoDB Hold the state that keeps compute stateless 1.4, 1.5 SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Step Functions Decouple and coordinate compute components 1.7, 6.3 CloudWatch, X-Ray, CloudTrail Metrics, logs, traces and audit Unit 7

Keep compute boring

In a good design, compute is stateless and replaceable, surrounded by managed services that hold the state, route the traffic and observe the behaviour. If compute is the most complicated part of your diagram, responsibilities are probably in the wrong place.

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Instance type / family A vCPU-memory-network combination (m7g.large); families group types by workload Graviton AWS ARM-based processor; needs arm64 builds Nitro System AWS hardware and lightweight hypervisor behind modern EC2 Firecracker microVM Minimal VM that isolates each Lambda environment and Fargate task Instance profile Delivers an IAM role to an EC2 instance IMDSv2 Token-based Instance Metadata Service; blocks SSRF credential theft Launch template Versioned instance configuration used by Auto Scaling groups Task definition / Task ECS blueprint / a running copy of it Task execution role / Task role Role used by ECS infrastructure / role used by your code Pod Smallest Kubernetes unit: one or more containers sharing a network Execution environment The microVM running a Lambda function, one request at a time Cold start Invocation that pays the cost of creating a new environment Reserved / provisioned concurrency Cap-and-guarantee / pre-warmed environments Event source mapping Lambda poller for queues and streams Control plane / data plane Management layer / layer that runs workloads and serves traffic Bin packing Placing workloads on hosts to maximise utilisation

docs.title: EC2
docs.text: Instance family, purchase option and scaling policy are covered in the EC2 deep dive above. In addition: prefer arm64 (Graviton) where dependencies allow, use gp3 EBS volumes by default (io2 for high, consistent IOPS; instance store for scratch only), set the ASG health check to ELB, and always require IMDSv2.

docs.title: Lambda
docs.text:
Setting Options Guidance Memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB Tune with Power Tuning Architecture x86_64 or arm64 arm64 where dependencies allow Timeout 1 s to 900 s Slightly above observed p99, never "maximum to be safe" Packaging ZIP or container image Image for large dependencies Concurrency Unreserved, reserved, provisioned Reserved to protect databases; provisioned for latency-critical paths VPC None, or subnets and security groups Attach only to reach private resources Error handling Retries, DLQ, on-failure destination Always capture failed asynchronous events

ECS settings are covered in 2.2 and 2.3; EKS settings in 3.1 and 3.3.

docs.title: Choosing a compute service
docs.text:
Work through the questions in order. The first constraint that applies decides the answer.

flowchart TD
    S["Start: characterise the workload"] --> Q1{"Does it require OS level control, GPUs, licensed per host software, or a custom kernel"}
    Q1 -->|"Yes"| EC2["Amazon EC2"]
    Q1 -->|"No"| Q2{"Is the work event driven, short lived, and under 15 minutes"}
    Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"Is cold start latency acceptable or mitigable"}
    Q3 -->|"Yes"| LAM["AWS Lambda"]
    Q3 -->|"No"| Q4
    Q2 -->|"No"| Q4{"Is the application containerised or containerisable"}
    Q4 -->|"No"| EC2
    Q4 -->|"Yes"| Q5{"Does the team need Kubernetes portability, extensibility, or existing K8s tooling"}
    Q5 -->|"Yes"| EKS["Amazon EKS"]
    Q5 -->|"No"| ECS["Amazon ECS"]
    ECS --> Q6{"Do you need host access, GPUs, or very high steady utilisation"}
    EKS --> Q6
    Q6 -->|"Yes"| EC2CAP["Run on EC2 capacity"]
    Q6 -->|"No"| FAR["Run on AWS Fargate"]

Apply the framework

A nightly report job reads 40 GB from S3 and runs for 40 minutes. Lambda is ruled out by the 15-minute limit. The job is containerisable, stateless and needs no host control, so an ECS task on Fargate, triggered by EventBridge Scheduler, fits. If it needed GPUs, it would move to AWS Batch on EC2 Spot.

docs.title: Comparison matrix
docs.text:
This table also serves as the advantages and limitations of each service.

Dimension EC2 ECS on Fargate EKS Lambda Operational burden Highest Low High Lowest Billing Per instance-second Per task-second Cluster fee plus nodes Per millisecond Idle cost Full Full while task runs Cluster fee plus nodes Zero Scaling speed Minutes Tens of seconds Seconds (Pods), minutes (nodes) Milliseconds to seconds Maximum duration Unlimited Unlimited Unlimited 15 minutes Portability off AWS Low Medium (images port) High Low Skills needed Linux administration Docker and AWS Deep Kubernetes Code and event design Main advantage Full OS control, widest hardware choice No nodes; free control plane Kubernetes ecosystem and portability No infrastructure, zero idle cost Main limitation You patch the OS; slow to scale Higher unit price; no GPUs or DaemonSets Complexity, cluster fee, mandatory upgrades 15-minute limit, cold starts, payload limits Best fit Legacy, licensed, GPU, steady heavy load Microservices, small ops team Large multi-team platforms Event glue, APIs, spiky work

docs.title: Scalability and availability
docs.text:
• Know the bottleneck. More compute is useless if the database runs out of connections, which is exactly what happens when 1,000 concurrent Lambda functions hit RDS. Use RDS Proxy or a queue in between.
  • Scaling latency sets your headroom. Lambda reacts in seconds, Fargate tasks in tens of seconds, EC2 instances in minutes. Slower scaling needs more spare capacity.
  • Spread across at least two, preferably three, AZs. This is the highest-value availability decision.
  • Treat every node as disposable. Handle SIGTERM, finish in-flight requests, and deregister from the load balancer before exiting.
  • Run at least two copies of everything. One replica has no availability during a deployment or node drain.

The architect's default

For a new, containerisable, stateless service with no unusual needs, start with ECS on Fargate, with Lambda for event glue. Move to EKS when several teams need a shared, extensible platform or genuine multi-cloud portability. Move to EC2 when a hard constraint forces it. "We might need Kubernetes later" is speculation, not a constraint.

docs.title: AWS Best Practices
docs.text: Pillar Compute practice Operational excellence Define all infrastructure as code (5.3); make deployments small and reversible; automate patching or remove it with immutable AMIs and Fargate Security One IAM role per instance, task, Pod or function; no long-lived keys; compute in private subnets; IMDSv2 required Reliability Multi-AZ by default; health-based replacement; queues to absorb downstream failures; raise service quotas before launch Performance efficiency Choose instance family and Lambda memory from measurements; prefer Graviton; move non-urgent work out of the request path Cost optimisation Savings Plans for the steady baseline only; Spot for interruptible work; switch off non-production outside working hours Sustainability Higher utilisation means less energy per unit of work; Graviton does more work per watt; serverless uses nothing when idle

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Every compute service has a way to obtain temporary, automatically rotated credentials. Using anything else, such as access keys in code or images, is a defect.

Compute service Credential mechanism Granularity EC2 Instance profile, read through IMDSv2 Per instance ECS (EC2 or Fargate) Task execution role and task role Per task EKS Node role, plus EKS Pod Identity or IRSA Per Pod Lambda Execution role Per function

The node role anti-pattern in EKS

Permissions on the EKS node role are inherited by every Pod on that node. Keep the node role minimal and give each workload its own role. See 3.1 Amazon EKS Architecture.

Further compute-specific rules:

  • Private subnets. Only load balancers and NAT gateways belong in public subnets.
  • No SSH from the internet. Use Systems Manager Session Manager instead of opening port 22.
  • Secrets at runtime. Fetch from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store; never bake them into images or plaintext environment variables.
  • Harden containers. Run as non-root, scan images in ECR, and block vulnerable images in the pipeline.
  • Lambda in a VPC is not automatically more secure. Attach it only when it must reach private resources.

IAM is covered in 8.1, network security in 1.6 and 8.2, and encryption in 8.3.

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Performance.

  • Cache before computing: CloudFront at the edge, ElastiCache in front of the database.
  • Reuse connections. In Lambda, create SDK clients and database connections outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.
  • Scale on the real bottleneck. Request count per target for a web tier; queue depth or message age for a queue consumer. Scale out fast, scale in slowly.
  • Right-size with AWS Compute Optimizer, which covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda.

Cost.

Service You pay for Often overlooked EC2 Instance-seconds, EBS storage Unattached volumes and Elastic IPs, cross-AZ transfer ECS on EC2 The underlying instances Idle capacity from poor packing Fargate Requested vCPU and GB per second Over-sized tasks EKS Cluster fee plus data plane Extended-support surcharge, one load balancer per Ingress Lambda Requests and GB-seconds CloudWatch Logs, NAT for VPC functions, API Gateway

Match the purchase option to the shape of demand: Savings Plans for the steady baseline, scheduled scaling for predictable peaks, On-Demand with target tracking for unpredictable spikes, and Spot or Fargate Spot for interruptible work.

NAT and data transfer are the classic surprise

A NAT Gateway charges per hour and per GB processed. Containers pulling images from ECR, or Lambda calling S3, through NAT can cost more than the compute itself. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free; add them always.

Monitoring.

Service Key metrics What they reveal EC2 CPUUtilization, StatusCheckFailed, CPUCreditBalance Saturation, health, T-family credit exhaustion EC2 (agent) Memory and disk use The hypervisor cannot see inside the guest: install the CloudWatch agent ECS CPUUtilization, MemoryUtilization, running and pending task counts Sustained pending tasks mean not enough capacity Lambda Errors, Duration, Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions Throttles means a concurrency limit was hit

Every service should alarm on errors, latency, saturation, and failure to scale (pending tasks, unschedulable Pods or Lambda throttles). Monitoring is covered fully in Unit 7.

docs.title: Integration with Other AWS Services
docs.text:
The services compute depends on are listed under Architecture Components. Two integrations deserve a note: RDS Proxy protects relational databases from Lambda connection storms, and Step Functions runs workflows longer than Lambda's 15-minute limit. The diagram shows how the compute services combine in one system.

flowchart TD
    U["Users"] --> R53["Route 53"]
    R53 --> CF["CloudFront with WAF"]
    CF --> S3S["S3 static assets"]
    CF --> ALB["Application Load Balancer"]
    ALB --> SVC1["ECS Fargate: Orders service"]
    ALB --> SVC2["ECS Fargate: Catalog service"]
    SVC1 --> DDB["DynamoDB Orders table"]
    SVC2 --> RDS["Aurora Catalog cluster"]
    SVC1 --> EB["EventBridge OrderPlaced event"]
    EB --> SQS["SQS fulfilment queue"]
    EB --> SNSN["SNS notifications topic"]
    SQS --> LFUL["Lambda fulfilment processor"]
    SNSN --> LEMAIL["Lambda email sender"]
    LFUL --> SFN["Step Functions shipping workflow"]
    SFN --> ECSJOB["ECS task: label generation"]
    ECR["ECR"] --> SVC1
    ECR --> SVC2

Reading this diagram

The synchronous path (user, load balancer, service, database) is kept short. Everything that need not finish before responding, such as fulfilment, emails and shipping, runs behind EventBridge and SQS on Lambda or ECS tasks. Each component uses the compute service that fits its shape.

docs.text:
Compute choice follows the pattern. The patterns themselves are covered elsewhere.

Pattern Typical compute Covered in Three-tier web application EC2 ASG or ECS service behind an ALB 1.7 Microservices ECS or EKS, one service per team 4.1 Event-driven processing Lambda triggered by S3, SQS or EventBridge 1.7, 6.3 Queue-based load levelling ECS tasks or Lambda scaling on queue depth 1.7 Batch and scheduled jobs Fargate tasks, AWS Batch on Spot This topic Sidecar (logging, tracing, proxy) Extra container in the same task or Pod 2.1 Retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead Any; Lambda reserved concurrency acts as a bulkhead 4.3 Blue/green and canary deployment CodeDeploy for ECS and Lambda; Lambda alias weights 5.2

docs.title: Beginner Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it is wrong Do instead Thinking Fargate is an orchestrator It is a capacity mode for ECS and EKS Choose ECS or EKS first, then the capacity Thinking ECS costs more than EKS ECS has no control plane fee; EKS charges per cluster Compare total cost, not labels Application servers in public subnets Compute exposed to the internet Private subnets; only load balancers public Opening SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0 Invites brute-force attacks Systems Manager Session Manager Access keys in code, AMIs or images Long-lived credentials leak Instance profiles, task roles, execution roles Using the latest image tag Non-deterministic deploys, no clean rollback Immutable tags such as the Git commit SHA Writing state to a container's or instance's disk Lost on restart, scale-in or replacement; instance store is lost on stop S3, DynamoDB, RDS or EFS Confusing the task execution role with the task role Your code uses the task role Keep both minimal and separate Confusing reserved and provisioned concurrency Reserved caps and guarantees; provisioned pre-warms Use each for its purpose Using T instances for sustained high CPU Credits run out and the instance is throttled M or C families Running databases on compute-optimised C instances Too little memory per vCPU Memory-optimised R or X families Expecting memory metrics in EC2 by default The hypervisor cannot see guest memory Install the CloudWatch agent Assuming Lambda is always cheapest Steady high volume can cost more Model costs with real volumes Thinking Multi-AZ means multi-Region Multi-AZ is inside one Region Separate deployments plus Route 53 for multi-Region

docs.title: Production Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Do instead High-concurrency Lambda connecting straight to RDS Database connection exhaustion RDS Proxy, reserved concurrency or a queue No reserved concurrency anywhere One runaway function throttles every other function Reserve for critical functions; cap the rest No DLQ on asynchronous processing Events silently lost after retries DLQ or on-failure destination with an alarm ASG health check type left as EC2 Instances with a broken application stay in service Use ELB health checks Scaling on CPU when the bottleneck is a queue The system never scales when it should Scale on the metric that reflects the constraint No graceful shutdown Requests dropped at every deployment and scale-in Handle SIGTERM and drain Long Lambda timeouts "to be safe" A hung dependency bills up to 15 minutes per call Timeout slightly above observed p99 Not testing at the concurrency quota Throttling discovered on launch day Load-test and raise quotas in advance No rollback mechanism A bad release becomes a long outage Deployment circuit breaker, blue/green or canary

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
AWS compute is one spectrum of abstraction, not five unrelated products. EC2 gives full control and full responsibility. Lambda takes almost all responsibility in exchange for a constrained model. ECS and EKS sit in between, with Fargate available to remove the node layer.

Area Key lesson The spectrum Every step up trades control for less operational work. Pick the highest abstraction your constraints allow EC2 Choose the family by workload; Savings Plans for the baseline, Spot for interruptible work; ASGs across AZs with ELB health checks ECS, EKS, Fargate ECS is simple and free to run; EKS buys the Kubernetes ecosystem at the cost of complexity; Fargate is capacity, not an orchestrator Lambda Event-driven, per-millisecond, zero idle cost; 15-minute limit, cold starts, concurrency is shared Statelessness Elasticity, Spot, rolling deployments and multi-AZ resilience all depend on compute holding no durable state Security Temporary credentials per instance, task, Pod or function; compute in private subnets Cost Purchase model, Lambda memory, NAT and log retention are design decisions that show up on the bill later

Next: compute is only half the picture; the state it relies on lives in storage. 1.4 AWS Storage Services covers S3, EBS and EFS.

docs.title: Storage Services  Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, and Amazon EFS
docs.text:
Scope of this chapter

This is the Unit 1 survey of AWS storage: object, block and file storage, what S3, EBS and EFS each are, and how to choose between them. The full treatment of each service is in 6.1 AWS Storage Solutions: Amazon S3, Amazon EBS and Amazon EFS.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
AWS storage services are managed, API-driven services that keep data independent of any single compute resource. They form the data layer of an architecture: beneath compute (EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda) and alongside databases (RDS, DynamoDB, Aurora).

Three services form the foundation. Each implements a different storage abstraction.

Service Abstraction Scope In one sentence Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) Object Regional Stores whole objects (bytes plus metadata) in buckets, accessed over an HTTPS REST API, with effectively unlimited capacity and eleven nines of durability Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) Block One Availability Zone A network-attached disk for one EC2 instance, which the operating system formats (ext4, XFS, NTFS) like a physical disk; backed up by snapshots stored in S3 Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) File Regional (multi-AZ) A shared NFSv4.1 file system with directories, permissions and locking, mounted by thousands of clients at once; capacity grows and shrinks automatically Storage Services in AWS

Image Source: AI generated (Google Gemini)

Where the storage services fit in AWS architecture

Image Source: AI generated (Chatgpt)

Storage is not the same as a database

A database adds structure, queries, transactions and indexes on top of storage. A storage service stores bytes and returns bytes. If you need to query data by its content, use a database (1.5). If you need to retrieve data by its name, use storage.

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
docs.text:
In a traditional data centre, storage is bought years ahead, durability depends on RAID inside one building, and restores from tape take days. AWS storage replaces this with:

  • capacity provisioned by API, on demand;
  • multi-AZ durability as a default;
  • performance set independently of capacity (gp3 volumes);
  • incremental snapshots restorable in minutes;
  • access control by IAM identity rather than network location.

AWS offers three services because the three abstractions make incompatible trade-offs:

Abstraction Gives up To gain Object (S3) In-place updates Unbounded scale and durability Block (EBS) Sharing and cross-AZ reach Sub-millisecond random access File (EFS) Lower cost and latency Shared POSIX files across many hosts Storage service trade-offs

Image Source: AI generated (Chatgpt)

The architect's framing

Do not ask "which storage service should I use". Ask "what is the access pattern of my data". Access pattern determines abstraction; abstraction determines service. See 6.1 The Three Storage Abstractions.

docs.title: Object, block and file compared
docs.text:
Dimension Object storage (S3) Block storage (EBS) File storage (EFS) Unit of storage Object: bytes plus metadata Fixed-size block File in a directory tree Access HTTPS REST API Block device on one instance NFS mount from many clients Updates Replace the whole object Overwrite any block in place Read, write, seek, append Concurrent writers Many; last write wins per key Normally one instance Many, coordinated by the file system Typical latency Tens of milliseconds Sub-millisecond to low milliseconds Low milliseconds Scope Regional, three or more AZs One Availability Zone Regional (or One Zone) Storage service decision options

Image Source: AI generated (Google Gemini)

docs.title: Instance store
docs.text: Instance store is disk physically attached to the EC2 host. It is the fastest option but ephemeral: data is lost when the instance stops or terminates. Use it only for scratch space, caches and data replicated elsewhere.

docs.title: Durability is not availability
docs.text:
Property Meaning Example Durability Probability that data is not lost S3 Standard: eleven nines Availability Probability that data can be reached right now S3 Standard: 99.99 percent

A single EBS volume is replicated only within one AZ, so a zone failure makes it unavailable (though not lost).

Durability does not protect against deletion

Durability figures cover hardware failure only. A user or application that deletes data deletes it durably. Versioning, Object Lock and backups protect against that. Per-class figures: 6.1 Durability and Availability.

S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for object operations. Bucket configuration changes and cross-Region replication remain eventually consistent.

docs.title: AWS Service Deep Dive
docs.text: A summary of the options an architect chooses between. Full limits, pricing and features are in 6.1.

docs.title: Amazon S3 storage classes
docs.text:
Storage class Use when Minimum storage duration Retrieval S3 Standard Data is accessed frequently None Milliseconds S3 Intelligent-Tiering The access pattern is unknown or changes None Milliseconds S3 Standard-IA Read rarely, but needed immediately 30 days Milliseconds, per-GiB fee S3 One Zone-IA As above, and the data can be recreated 30 days Milliseconds, single AZ S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Archive that still needs millisecond access 90 days Milliseconds S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Archive; minutes to hours is acceptable 90 days Restore required S3 Glacier Deep Archive Long-term retention at the lowest price 180 days Restore in about 12 hours or more S3 Express One Zone Single-digit-millisecond latency at very high request rates One hour Single-AZ directory bucket

Colder is not always cheaper

Colder classes have minimum storage durations and retrieval fees. Moving short-lived or frequently read data into IA or Glacier can increase cost. See 6.1 Storage classes.

Other S3 features to recognise:

  • Versioning: every overwrite and delete keeps the previous version.
  • Lifecycle rules: transition or expire objects by age.
  • Object Lock: write-once-read-many retention.
  • Replication: asynchronous copy to another bucket or Region.
  • Presigned URLs: time-limited access to one object without sharing credentials.
  • Multipart upload: large objects uploaded in parallel parts.

docs.title: Amazon EBS volume types
docs.text:
Type Media Use when gp3 SSD The default: boot volumes, most databases and app servers; IOPS and throughput set independently of size gp2 SSD Legacy; performance tied to size. Migrate to gp3 io2 Block Express SSD Mission-critical databases needing the highest IOPS (up to 256,000) and lowest latency io1 SSD Legacy provisioned IOPS; superseded by io2 st1 HDD Large sequential reads: log processing, data warehouses sc1 HDD Cold data read a few times a month, at the lowest cost

EBS bills for provisioned capacity. Volumes can grow but not shrink, and performance is also capped by the instance type. See 6.1 Volume types.

docs.title: Amazon EFS options
docs.text:
Setting Options Default choice Throughput mode Elastic, Provisioned, Bursting Elastic Performance mode General Purpose, Max I/O General Purpose Storage class Standard, Infrequent Access, Archive (plus One Zone variants) Lifecycle management moves cold files to cheaper classes Availability Regional or One Zone One Zone only for recreatable data

See 6.1 Throughput modes, performance modes and elastic capacity.

docs.title: Related services
docs.text:
• Amazon FSx: managed file systems beyond EFS: Windows File Server (SMB, Active Directory), Lustre (HPC and ML, linked to S3), NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS.
  • AWS Storage Gateway: presents on-premises NFS, SMB, iSCSI or virtual tape interfaces backed by AWS storage, for hybrid and migration use.

See 6.1 Choosing between EFS, FSx and Mountpoint for Amazon S3.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text: Component Role in a storage architecture EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda Attach EBS, mount EFS and call the S3 API (1.3). Containers use EFS for shared volumes and EBS for per-task or per-pod volumes VPC endpoints, route tables Private path from compute to S3 (Gateway endpoint) and to EFS mount targets (1.6) Security groups Allow TCP 2049 from clients to EFS mount targets CloudFront Caches S3 objects at the edge; Origin Access Control keeps the bucket private IAM Authorises every storage API call (1.2) KMS Encrypts S3 objects, EBS volumes and EFS file systems (8.3) CloudWatch, CloudTrail Storage metrics, alarms and audit records AWS Backup Central backup policy for EBS, EFS and S3

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Bucket Regional container for S3 objects, with a globally unique name Key and prefix The full name of an object, and a leading part of it used for grouping. S3 has no real folders Storage class Per-object setting for cost, latency, availability and retrieval behaviour Lifecycle policy Rules that transition or expire objects by age Versioning Keeps every version of an object; a delete inserts a delete marker Volume An EBS block device in one Availability Zone IOPS Input/output operations per second Snapshot Incremental, point-in-time backup of an EBS volume, stored as a Regional resource Multi-Attach Attaching one io1/io2 volume to several instances in the same AZ Mount target Network interface in a subnet (one per AZ) through which clients reach EFS Access point EFS entry point enforcing a root directory and POSIX identity Gateway VPC endpoint Free, route-table-based private path from a VPC to S3

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Service Settings that matter first Sensible default S3 Storage class, versioning, encryption, Block Public Access, lifecycle, replication Versioning on, Block Public Access on, lifecycle rule for noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads EBS Type, size, IOPS and throughput, encryption, delete on termination, snapshots gp3, encrypted, snapshots automated by Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup EFS Throughput and performance mode, lifecycle, encryption, access points, mount targets Elastic, General Purpose, a mount target in every AZ, TLS mounts

Detailed tables: S3 bucket configuration, EBS configuration, EFS configuration.

docs.title: The decision framework
docs.text:
graph TD
    A["What storage does this workload need"] --> B{"Is the data needed after the compute instance dies"}
    B -->|"No, purely temporary"| C["Instance store or ephemeral container storage"]
    B -->|"Yes"| D{"Do multiple hosts need concurrent read and write access"}
    D -->|"Yes, POSIX required"| E{"Windows SMB or Active Directory"}
    E -->|"Yes"| F["Amazon FSx for Windows File Server"]
    E -->|"No"| G{"Extreme HPC throughput needed"}
    G -->|"Yes"| H["Amazon FSx for Lustre"]
    G -->|"No"| I["Amazon EFS"]
    D -->|"No, single host"| J{"Does the application require a block device or a POSIX file path"}
    J -->|"Yes"| K["Amazon EBS"]
    J -->|"No, API access is acceptable"| L{"Whole-object read and write"}
    L -->|"Yes"| M["Amazon S3"]
    L -->|"No, random in-place updates"| K

docs.title: When to choose each
docs.text:
Choose When Avoid when S3 Data is written whole and read by name: data lakes, backups, media, static assets, build artefacts, logs The application needs POSIX semantics or low-latency transactional writes EBS One instance needs a persistent disk: boot volumes, self-managed databases Data must be shared, or must stay accessible through an AZ failure EFS Many instances, containers or functions share files: CMS content, uploads, ML models, home directories Latency-critical databases, or workloads dominated by small metadata operations Instance store Scratch space, caches, data replicated elsewhere Anything that must survive a stop or termination

Scope determines availability

S3 and EFS survive the loss of an Availability Zone; a single EBS volume does not. Going beyond one Region always needs asynchronous replication (S3 replication, EFS replication, snapshot copies), so a multi-Region design always has a non-zero Recovery Point Objective.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Access control. S3 access combines IAM identity policies, bucket policies and Block Public Access; an explicit Deny anywhere wins. Keep ACLs disabled. Never make a bucket public to host a website; use CloudFront with Origin Access Control. See 1.2 and 8.1.
  • Encryption. New S3 objects are encrypted by default with SSE-S3; SSE-KMS adds key control and an audit trail. EBS and EFS encrypt at rest with KMS; EFS encrypts in transit with TLS via efs-utils. See 8.3 S3 encryption choices.
  • Network isolation. Use a Gateway VPC endpoint for S3. Restrict EFS mount targets to TCP 2049 from the application's security group.
  • Audit. CloudTrail records management events by default; S3 object-level data events must be enabled explicitly.

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Service Performance Main cost driver Cost lever Metrics to watch S3 Multipart upload and byte-range reads in parallel; CloudFront caching; avoid millions of tiny objects Storage class, requests, data transfer out Lifecycle transitions, fewer larger objects, Gateway endpoint instead of NAT 4xxErrors, 5xxErrors, FirstByteLatency, BucketSizeBytes EBS SSD for random I/O, HDD for sequential; the instance's EBS bandwidth is often the real ceiling Provisioned capacity, used or not Right-size, delete unattached volumes, gp2 to gp3, snapshot retention VolumeQueueLength, BurstBalance, VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps EFS Elastic throughput and parallel clients; avoid very large directories Data in the Standard class Lifecycle to Infrequent Access and Archive PercentIOLimit, BurstCreditBalance, ClientConnections

The two practices with the highest return

  1. S3 versioning plus a lifecycle rule expiring noncurrent versions. Accidental deletion becomes an inconvenience, not a disaster, at bounded cost.
  2. A Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 in every VPC. It is free, improves security, and often removes a large NAT Gateway bill.

Other habits: define storage as code, tag everything, automate snapshots and test restores, and copy backups to another account and Region. CloudWatch itself is covered in 7.1.

docs.title: Common Architecture Patterns
docs.text: Pattern How it works Externalised state App servers keep no durable state: uploads in S3, shared files in EFS, sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB. This makes the tier horizontally scalable (1.7) Static website, private origin S3 holds the assets; CloudFront serves them Event-driven processing An S3 upload emits an event to Lambda, SNS, SQS or EventBridge, which writes a derived object Direct upload Browsers upload to S3 with presigned URLs; the app tier never handles the bytes Data lake S3 as the landing zone, queried in place by Athena, Glue or EMR Container volumes EFS gives shared ReadWriteMany volumes; EBS gives ReadWriteOnce volumes bound to one AZ Isolated backups Snapshots and backups copied to another account and Region to survive credential compromise

docs.title: Advantages and Limitations
docs.text: Advantages Limitations Durability far beyond what one organisation can engineer S3 has no POSIX semantics and is too slow for transactional writes Elasticity: S3 and EFS have no size to provision EBS is confined to one AZ and bills for provisioned capacity Storage separated from compute, so compute can be replaced or run on Spot EFS costs more per GiB, has higher latency than EBS, and is weak on metadata-heavy workloads Performance decoupled from capacity (gp3) Cross-Region replication is always asynchronous Security tied to IAM identity and audited by CloudTrail Lifecycle transitions run roughly daily; cold classes have minimum durations

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Do instead Believing S3 has folders, so a "folder rename" is cheap Treat keys as flat names; a rename copies every object Making a bucket public to serve a website CloudFront with Origin Access Control Attaching an EBS volume to an instance in another AZ Snapshot it and restore in the target AZ Mounting EFS without opening TCP 2049 Allow 2049 from the client security group Using EFS or S3 as a transactional database's data directory EBS, or a managed database (1.5) Versioning without a lifecycle rule Expire noncurrent versions Routing S3 traffic through a NAT gateway Gateway VPC endpoint Leaving unattached volumes and old snapshots Regular clean-up and snapshot retention rules

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The storage decision comes before the compute decision. Three ideas carry beyond AWS:

Idea Key lesson Access pattern determines abstraction Object (S3), block (EBS) and file (EFS) make incompatible trade-offs. Know how data is read and written, and the service follows Scope determines availability S3 and EFS are Regional and survive an AZ loss. EBS is bound to one AZ; instance store to one host Durability is not availability Neither protects against deletion; versioning, Object Lock and backups do Settings are dials, not defaults Storage classes, volume types, throughput modes, lifecycle, replication and encryption are chosen against explicit requirements Cheapest high-value habits Versioning plus lifecycle; Gateway endpoint for S3; gp3; delete unattached volumes
