Container platforms (Units 2 and 3) need EBS and EFS volumes; serverless designs are triggered by S3 events; pipelines store artefacts in S3. 6.1 AWS Storage Solutions returns to all three services in depth.

Next: 1.5 AWS Database Services covers the services that add structure and queries on top of storage.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: Database Services on AWS  Amazon RDS and Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon ElastiCache
Definition
docs.text:
A managed database service is a database whose infrastructure AWS operates for you: hardware, operating system and engine patching, backups, failure detection and failover. You keep responsibility for the data model, queries, indexes, access control and capacity or cost decisions.

This chapter covers three services, each with a different job:

Service Category Data model Primary purpose Amazon RDS Managed relational database Relational, SQL, ACID Structured transactional data with relationships and joins Amazon Aurora Cloud-native relational engine (an RDS option) MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible Relational workloads needing higher throughput, faster recovery and auto-growing storage Amazon DynamoDB Managed NoSQL database Key-value and document Single-digit millisecond access at any scale for known access patterns Amazon ElastiCache Managed in-memory store In-memory key-value and data structures Microsecond reads, offloading the primary database, sessions and leaderboards

Scope of this chapter

This is the Unit 1 survey: the concepts you need to choose a database, and each service at summary level. The full treatment of RDS, Aurora and DynamoDB (and of Amazon Neptune and Amazon Redshift) is in 6.2 AWS Database Services. ElastiCache is covered in depth in 6.1.

The data tier is the stateful tier

In a well-designed cloud-native system the compute tier is stateless: instances can be destroyed and recreated freely. State lives in the database, and state is what makes distributed systems hard. Scaling stateless compute is easy (add instances behind a load balancer). Scaling state forces explicit decisions about consistency, partitioning and replication. This is why the data tier usually sets the ceiling of an architecture.

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
Running a database yourself is hard
docs.text:
Self-managing a production database means owning provisioning, OS and engine patching, backups and restore tests, replication and failover, monitoring, capacity planning and security. None of this differentiates the business. AWS calls it undifferentiated heavy lifting, and removing it is the core value of managed databases.

Dimension Self-managed AWS managed Time to first database Weeks Minutes High availability Weeks of replication and failover engineering Enable Multi-AZ Failover time Often manual, minutes to hours Typically 60 to 120 seconds for RDS Multi-AZ; around 30 seconds or less for Aurora Backups and point-in-time recovery Custom scripts and log shipping Automated, to any second within the retention window Read scaling Manual replica configuration Add a read replica with a few API calls Encryption at rest Disk- or engine-level setup Enable at creation, integrated with KMS

Managed does not mean AWS handles everything

AWS will faithfully replicate a badly designed schema and back up a table with no indexes. It will not tell you that a query does a full table scan, that a partition key causes a hot partition, or that your application role is over-privileged. Under the shared responsibility model, design is your responsibility, and poor design is what usually causes outages.

docs.title: Purpose-built databases
docs.text:
The second reason is architectural: the relational model is not optimal for every workload. A shopping cart, a social graph, IoT telemetry, a search index and a financial ledger have different access patterns, consistency needs and scaling behaviour. AWS therefore offers a family of purpose-built databases and expects architects to choose deliberately.

graph TD
    A["Workload"] --> B{"Shape of data and access pattern"}
    B -->|"Rows, joins, transactions"| C["Relational - RDS or Aurora"]
    B -->|"Key-value at massive scale"| D["Key-value - DynamoDB"]
    B -->|"Microsecond latency, ephemeral"| E["In-memory - ElastiCache"]
    B -->|"Highly connected relationships"| F["Graph - Neptune"]
    B -->|"Analytical scans over history"| G["Data warehouse - Redshift"]
    B -->|"Full-text search"| H["Search - OpenSearch Service"]

Choose by access pattern, but do not over-fragment

Choose the database that matches the access pattern, not the one you already know: changing a data model after production data exists usually means a rewrite. Equally, every extra data store adds backups, monitoring, credentials and a consistency boundary. Add a new store only when the workload demonstrably does not fit the ones you have.

docs.title: Relational databases and ACID
docs.text:
A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed schema, links them with foreign keys, and uses SQL so that joins and filters can be decided at query time. Its contract is ACID:

Property Meaning Example Atomicity A transaction completes fully or not at all A transfer cannot debit one account without crediting the other Consistency Every transaction respects all constraints Foreign keys and uniqueness are never violated Isolation Concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate state Two simultaneous stock decrements cannot both oversell Durability Committed data survives crashes An acknowledged order is not lost if the instance dies

Isolation is a dial, not a switch. SQL defines levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable); stronger levels cost throughput. PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed and MySQL InnoDB to Repeatable Read.

docs.title: NoSQL and BASE
docs.text:
NoSQL databases relax a relational constraint (fixed schema, joins, or strict consistency) in exchange for horizontal scale and predictable latency. Their typical posture is BASE:

  • Basically Available: every request gets a response, possibly not the latest data.
  • Soft state: state may change as replicas converge.
  • Eventually consistent: with no new writes, all replicas converge to the same value.

NoSQL does not mean no consistency

DynamoDB offers strongly consistent reads per request and ACID transactions across up to 100 items. Conversely, a relational database read through an asynchronous replica is eventually consistent. BASE describes a default, not an absolute limit.

docs.title: Vertical versus horizontal scaling
docs.text:
Aspect Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out) Method Bigger machine More machines Natural fit Relational writer Key-value stores, stateless compute Ceiling The largest instance type Effectively none Downtime Usually a restart or failover None if designed for it Complexity Low High: needs a partitioning strategy

The single-writer ceiling

A relational database's write path scales vertically. Read replicas scale reads, but there is one writer on one machine. DynamoDB scales writes horizontally by adding partitions, which is why it can absorb workloads no single relational instance could.

docs.title: The CAP theorem
docs.text:
The CAP theorem says a distributed data store cannot guarantee all three of the following at once:

Guarantee Precise meaning Consistency (C) Every read returns the most recent write or an error (linearizability, not the "C" in ACID) Availability (A) Every request gets a non-error response, possibly stale Partition tolerance (P) The system keeps working when messages between nodes are lost

CA is not an option for a distributed system

Network partitions are a fact of physical networks, not a design choice, so any distributed system must tolerate them. The practical statement of CAP is: when a partition occurs, choose between consistency and availability.

Service Behaviour under partition Leaning RDS Multi-AZ Fails over to the synchronous standby; writes unavailable during failover CP Aurora Quorum-based storage across three AZs CP with high availability DynamoDB, eventually consistent reads Any replica may answer AP DynamoDB, strongly consistent reads Must reach the partition leader CP for those requests ElastiCache with replicas Failover can lose recent unreplicated writes AP, not durable by design

docs.title: PACELC  The Extension That Matters More in Practice
docs.text:
CAP only describes behaviour during a partition, which is rare. PACELC extends it:

If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency.

The "else" branch is what you meet every day. A strongly consistent DynamoDB read costs twice the capacity of an eventually consistent read and has higher latency, because the partition leader must serve it. A read replica is faster and offloads the primary but may return stale data. Almost every read path trades latency for consistency.

Using PACELC in a design review

For each read path ask: what does it cost the business if this data is slightly stale? A product description: nothing. A user's profile just after they edited it: it looks like a bug. An account balance before a withdrawal: unacceptable. Paths in one application can legitimately choose differently.

docs.title: OLTP Versus OLAP
docs.text:
Characteristic OLTP (transaction processing) OLAP (analytical processing) Typical operation Read or write a few rows by key Scan and aggregate millions of rows Latency target Milliseconds Seconds to minutes Concurrency Thousands of short transactions Few long queries Storage layout Row-oriented Column-oriented Example "Insert this order" "Revenue by region by month for three years" AWS services RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB Redshift, Athena, EMR

Do not run analytics on the production OLTP database

A large report can saturate I/O or hold locks, exhaust connection pools, and take the checkout path down with it. Separate the workloads: a dedicated reporting replica, an export to S3 queried with Athena, or a load into Redshift (Aurora offers zero-ETL integration with Redshift for this).

docs.title: Consistency models
docs.text: Model Guarantee Where you see it Strong A read reflects all prior writes RDS primary, Aurora writer, DynamoDB strongly consistent read Eventual A read may be stale; replicas converge DynamoDB default read, RDS read replica, Aurora reader Read-your-own-writes A client always sees its own writes Route that client's reads to the primary for a short window after a write

docs.title: Durability, availability, RPO and RTO
docs.text:
Durability is the likelihood that committed data is not lost. Availability is the proportion of time the system can serve requests. They are different: data can be safely stored across three AZs while the database is unreachable during failover, and ElastiCache can answer every request yet lose everything on restart.

Term Meaning Example Availability Uptime in "nines" 99.99 percent is roughly 52 minutes of downtime per year RPO (Recovery Point Objective) Maximum acceptable data loss, in time "We can lose at most 5 minutes of transactions" RTO (Recovery Time Objective) Maximum acceptable downtime "We must be serving within 15 minutes"

RPO and RTO drive the design

RPO 5 minutes and RTO 1 hour: automated backups with point-in-time recovery. RPO near zero and RTO under 2 minutes: Multi-AZ synchronous replication with automatic failover. Survive a Region loss: Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables. Always extract these two numbers before designing.

docs.title: Caching basics
docs.text:
A cache is a fast store holding a subset of data so repeat requests avoid the origin. It works because of locality: a small fraction of items receives most requests.

Term Meaning Hit / miss The item was / was not in the cache Hit ratio Hits divided by total requests; the key measure of effectiveness TTL Time after which an entry expires Eviction policy Which entries to discard when memory is full, for example LRU Invalidation Removing or updating an entry when the source data changes Stampede Many requests miss at once and all hit the database together

Why hit ratio matters so much

With a 0.5 ms cache read and a 10 ms database read, a 95 percent hit ratio averages 0.95 × 0.5 + 0.05 × 10 = 0.975 ms. At 80 percent it is 0.8 × 0.5 + 0.2 × 10 = 2.4 ms, about 2.5 times worse.

docs.title: AWS Service Deep Dive
docs.text: Each service is summarised at Unit 1 level. Full deep dives: 6.2 for RDS, Aurora and DynamoDB; 6.1 for ElastiCache.

docs.title: Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora
docs.text:
Purpose. A managed relational database with full SQL, ACID transactions and the existing tooling ecosystem, without the operational burden.

Engines. Aurora (MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible), MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and IBM Db2. For a new application with no licence constraint, Aurora PostgreSQL is the usual default.

Feature What it gives you Multi-AZ Synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover (availability, not read scaling) Read replicas Asynchronous readable copies for read scaling; up to 15 Aurora Replicas per cluster Automated backups and PITR Restore to any second within a 1 to 35 day retention window Encryption with KMS Chosen at creation; cannot be enabled in place RDS Proxy Managed connection pooling for Lambda and highly elastic compute Aurora storage Six copies across three AZs, self-healing, grows automatically, shared by all instances Aurora Serverless v2 Capacity that scales in fine-grained Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) Aurora Global Database Cross-Region replication, typically with sub-second lag

The shared limit is a single writer: reads scale out with replicas, writes scale up. See 6.2 for engines, pricing, limits and configurations.

The Lambda and RDS connection problem

A relational database supports a limited number of connections (a few hundred on a small instance). A Lambda function at 1,000 concurrent executions, each opening its own connection, exhausts that limit and breaks every other service sharing the database. Remedies: RDS Proxy, creating the connection outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it, reserved concurrency, or DynamoDB, which has no connections. See 6.2.

docs.title: Amazon DynamoDB
docs.text:
Purpose. A fully managed, serverless key-value and document database with consistent single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, no servers and no connections to manage.

Concept Summary Table, item, attribute Regional table of items, each up to 400 KB; no schema beyond the primary key Primary key A partition key alone, or partition key plus sort key Secondary indexes GSI: any keys, add any time, eventually consistent. LSI: same partition key, created only with the table, supports strong reads Capacity modes On-demand (pay per request) or provisioned (RCU and WCU, with auto scaling) Capacity units 1 RCU = one strongly consistent read per second up to 4 KB (or two eventually consistent); 1 WCU = one write per second up to 1 KB Transactions ACID across up to 100 items, at twice the capacity cost Other features TTL, Streams, Global Tables, point-in-time recovery, DAX

Model the access patterns before the data

Relational design starts with entities, because SQL can express any query later. DynamoDB design starts with a written list of every access pattern, and the key schema is derived from it. A poor partition key (for example status, where all ACTIVE items land together) cannot scale no matter how much capacity you buy, and fixing it later means a data migration.

See 6.2 for key and index design, single-table design and capacity arithmetic.

docs.title: Amazon ElastiCache
docs.text:
Purpose. Managed in-memory stores (Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached) that sit in front of a database or hold shared ephemeral state, serving hot data from RAM in microseconds instead of from disk in milliseconds.

A Valkey or Redis OSS deployment is a replication group of one shard or many (cluster mode), each a primary with asynchronous replicas; ElastiCache Serverless removes node sizing. Because replication is asynchronous, failover can lose recent writes, so ElastiCache is never the system of record.

Dimension Valkey / Redis OSS Memcached Data structures Strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, geospatial Strings only Replication, Multi-AZ failover Yes No Persistence and backup Yes (snapshots to S3) No Threading Largely single-threaded command execution Multi-threaded Typical use Sessions, leaderboards, rate limiting, caching Simple, high-throughput object caching

Default to Valkey or Redis OSS

Choose Memcached only for a simple, disposable, multi-threaded object cache where losing everything is acceptable. Otherwise replication, failover and richer data structures make Valkey or Redis OSS the better default.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text:
The data tier is more than the database itself.

Component Responsibility Private subnets Hold RDS, Aurora and ElastiCache. Databases never go in public subnets DB subnet group / cache subnet group Subnets in at least two AZs where RDS or ElastiCache may place nodes; required for Multi-AZ Security groups Allow the engine port only from the application tier's security group VPC gateway endpoint Private, no-charge route to DynamoDB (and S3) without a NAT gateway Aurora cluster Shared storage volume plus one writer and up to 15 readers RDS Proxy Pools connections between elastic compute and RDS or Aurora DynamoDB table, partitions, indexes Regional container; partitions are the unit of storage and throughput DynamoDB Streams Ordered change log that triggers Lambda for event-driven integration Secrets Manager, KMS, CloudWatch Credentials with rotation; encryption keys; metrics and alarms 
graph TD
    APP["Compute tier - ECS, EKS, EC2 or Lambda (private subnets)"]
    APP --> CACHE["ElastiCache replication group"]
    APP --> PROXY["RDS Proxy"]
    PROXY --> AUR["Aurora cluster - writer and readers"]
    CACHE -.->|"cache miss"| AUR
    APP --> GWEP["VPC gateway endpoint"]
    GWEP --> DDB["DynamoDB"]
    DDB --> STR["DynamoDB Streams"]
    STR --> LAM["Lambda consumer"]
    APP --> SM["Secrets Manager"]
    AUR --> S3["S3 - backups"]

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning ACID / BASE Relational transactional guarantees / the eventual-consistency posture of many NoSQL systems ACU Aurora Capacity Unit, the scaling unit of Aurora Serverless v2 Aurora cluster volume Shared storage replicated six ways across three AZs Capacity mode DynamoDB on-demand or provisioned throughput Cluster endpoint DNS name that always points at the current writer DAX DynamoDB Accelerator, a write-through in-memory cache for DynamoDB DB subnet group Subnets across AZs in which RDS may place instances Global Secondary Index (GSI) Index with different keys from the table, its own capacity, eventually consistent Global Table Multi-Region, multi-active DynamoDB table using last-writer-wins IAM role Identity assumed by a service or application to call AWS APIs (8.1) Item / item collection One DynamoDB record (max 400 KB) / all items sharing a partition key value KMS AWS Key Management Service, which manages encryption keys (8.3) Local Secondary Index (LSI) Index sharing the table's partition key with a different sort key; created with the table Multi-AZ Synchronous standby in a second AZ for automatic failover OLTP / OLAP Short transactional operations / large analytical scans Partition key / sort key Attribute whose hash places an item / attribute that orders items within a partition PITR Point-in-time recovery to any second within the retention window Projection Attributes copied into a secondary index: KEYS_ONLY, INCLUDE or ALL RCU / WCU DynamoDB read capacity unit (4 KB strong read) / write capacity unit (1 KB write) RDS Proxy Managed connection pool in front of RDS or Aurora Read replica / replica lag Asynchronous read-only copy / delay before a write appears on it Replication group ElastiCache primary nodes and their replicas, optionally sharded Scan versus Query Scan reads every item; Query reads only items with one partition key value Security group Stateful virtual firewall attached to a network interface Sparse index GSI containing only items that have the index key attribute Streams Time-ordered log of item changes in a DynamoDB table TTL Automatic expiry of a DynamoDB item or cache entry VPC Isolated virtual network in which RDS, Aurora and ElastiCache run (1.6) Writer / reader endpoints Aurora DNS names for the writer and for load-balanced readers

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
These decisions are made at creation and are expensive to change. Full option tables are in 6.2 for RDS and Aurora and DynamoDB, and in 6.1 for ElastiCache.

Service Decisions that matter most RDS and Aurora Engine and version; instance class or Serverless v2 ACU range; Multi-AZ for production; backup retention (zero disables PITR); encryption at creation; deletion protection DynamoDB Primary key; capacity mode; secondary indexes and projections; PITR; TTL attribute; Streams; Global Tables ElastiCache Engine; node-based or Serverless; cluster mode; Multi-AZ with automatic failover; eviction policy; encryption

docs.title: Which database do I choose?
docs.text: Requirement in a design or exam question Choose Relational data, joins, ACID transactions, an existing SQL application RDS, or Aurora for higher throughput, faster failover and auto-growing storage Key-value access at any scale, serverless, unpredictable traffic DynamoDB Access patterns not yet known, ad hoc queries likely A relational database Microsecond reads in front of a database, sessions, leaderboards ElastiCache, or DAX when the database is DynamoDB Improve read performance Read replicas or a cache, not Multi-AZ Improve availability or add automatic failover Multi-AZ, not read replicas Recover from an accidental deletion PITR or backups, not replication (it copies the deletion) Survive the loss of a Region Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables Deep relationship traversal, such as fraud rings Amazon Neptune (6.2) Aggregations over large history Amazon Redshift (6.2)

docs.title: Service comparison
docs.text:
Dimension RDS Aurora DynamoDB ElastiCache Query flexibility Full SQL Full SQL Key and index lookups only Key lookups and data-structure commands Write scaling Vertical, one writer Vertical, one writer Horizontal by partition Horizontal by shard Typical latency Low milliseconds Low milliseconds Single-digit milliseconds Sub-millisecond Durability Synchronous standby, backups Six copies across three AZs Synchronous replication across three AZs Weak by design Availability Multi-AZ failover, 1 to 2 minutes Failover typically under 30 seconds Built in; no visible failover Replica promotion; app must survive cache loss Connection model Persistent TCP Persistent TCP Stateless HTTPS Persistent TCP Network placement Private subnets Private subnets Regional endpoint via gateway endpoint Private subnets

The question to ask before choosing DynamoDB

Can you list every access pattern the application will need? If yes, DynamoDB serves them at any scale. If not, a relational database absorbs that uncertainty far more gracefully. DynamoDB moves design effort forward: more thinking before the first write, less firefighting at scale.

docs.title: Cache-Aside with a Read-Through Fallback
docs.text:
The default pattern for read-heavy applications. The application checks ElastiCache or DAX first; on a miss it reads the database and stores the result with a TTL. Only requested data is cached, and if the cache fails the application still works, only slower. Write-through, TTL design and stampede protection are in 6.1.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Cache as ElastiCache
    participant DB as Aurora
    App->>Cache: GET product:42
    alt Cache hit
        Cache-->>App: value
    else Cache miss
        Cache-->>App: null
        App->>DB: SELECT ... WHERE id = 42
        DB-->>App: row
        App->>Cache: SET product:42 (with TTL)
    end

docs.title: Read replica fan-out
docs.text: One writer and several readers, with read-only traffic sent to the reader endpoint. Reads that must reflect the caller's own write go to the writer. Aurora replicas share the storage volume, so lag is typically tens of milliseconds.

docs.title: Polyglot persistence
docs.text:
Choose the store per access pattern: Aurora for orders and payments, DynamoDB for high-volume key access, ElastiCache for sessions and hot reads, OpenSearch for search (often fed from DynamoDB Streams, because DynamoDB is not a search engine), S3 for large objects, Redshift for analytics.

Service-level data patterns (database per service, saga, CQRS, event sourcing) are covered in 1.7 Cloud-Native Design Patterns and 4.1.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Two layers. IAM controls the control plane (create, modify, delete a database). Database users control the data plane (who can SELECT which table). rds:* does not grant a SELECT. DynamoDB is the exception: every GetItem and PutItem is an IAM action, so access can be restricted per table, index or even per partition key (6.2).
  • Network isolation. Private subnets only; security group rules that reference the application security group, not CIDR ranges; DynamoDB through a gateway endpoint.
  • Credentials. Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, or IAM database authentication (short-lived tokens, no stored password). Never hard-code credentials.
  • Encryption. KMS at rest and TLS in transit. DynamoDB is always encrypted at rest; for RDS and ElastiCache it is a creation-time choice (encrypting later means snapshot, encrypted copy, restore).
  • Least privilege inside the database. Separate accounts for migrations, runtime and reporting.

Deeper treatment: IAM in 8.1, KMS and Secrets Manager in 8.3.

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Performance.

  • Cache the hot working set; set TTLs from tolerable staleness.
  • Send read-only traffic to replicas; use RDS Proxy for elastic compute.
  • Index for known queries (each index slows writes); confirm plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  • In DynamoDB, request paths use Query or GetItem, never Scan.

Cost.

Service Main cost drivers Key lever RDS / Aurora Instance or ACU hours, storage, I/O, backups, licences Right-size; Reserved Instances for steady load; stop non-production databases DynamoDB Requests or provisioned capacity, storage, optional features On-demand for spiky traffic; provisioned with auto scaling once steady; TTL to expire old items ElastiCache Node hours or serverless usage Size to the working set; a cache is usually cheaper than the larger database it replaces All Cross-AZ transfer, NAT processing, orphaned snapshots Gateway endpoints; snapshot and log retention policies

Figures change; check the AWS Pricing Calculator before committing to a budget.

Monitoring.

Service Metrics to alarm on Why RDS / Aurora DatabaseConnections, FreeStorageSpace, ReplicaLag, CPUUtilization Exhausted connections and full disks are the commonest hard outages DynamoDB ThrottledRequests, read and write throttle events Throttling signals under-provisioning or a hot partition ElastiCache CacheHitRate, Evictions, EngineCPUUtilization Rising evictions with falling hits means the cache is too small

Performance Insights (RDS/Aurora) and Contributor Insights (DynamoDB hot keys) help diagnose. CloudWatch is covered in 7.1.

docs.title: Advantages and Limitations
docs.text:
Service Advantages Limitations RDS Removes patching, backups, failover and replica setup while keeping SQL, tools and skills Writes scale vertically; failover is not instantaneous, so apps must retry; replicas are asynchronous Aurora Shared self-healing storage: cheap replicas, fast failover, automatic storage growth Still a single writer; higher ceiling, not none DynamoDB Consistent latency at any size; nothing to size, patch or fail over; on-demand needs no forecast No joins or ad hoc queries; access patterns fixed up front; 400 KB items; Global Tables use last-writer-wins ElastiCache Large latency gains and much less database load at small cost; rich data structures Not durable; invalidation is hard; memory is a hard limit; one more component to fail

There is no free scalability

DynamoDB's horizontal scale costs query flexibility. Aurora's rich queries cost a write ceiling. ElastiCache's speed costs durability. The architect chooses which price the workload can afford.

docs.title: Beginner Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it is wrong Do instead Making an RDS instance publicly accessible Exposes the database to the internet Private subnets and security group references Hard-coding credentials They leak through source control and logs Secrets Manager or IAM database authentication Using Scan in DynamoDB Reads and bills every item Design keys so access is Query or GetItem Backup retention of zero Disables PITR Set retention deliberately Treating ElastiCache as durable Data lost on failover or eviction Cache only what can be rebuilt Using Multi-AZ to scale reads The standby is for failover Read replicas or a cache

docs.title: Production Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Remedy Lambda connecting directly to RDS at high concurrency Connection exhaustion and cascading failure RDS Proxy, reserved concurrency, connection reuse Never testing failover or restore Recovery is an assumption Regular failover and restore drills Analytics on the OLTP database Checkout slows or fails Reporting replica, S3 plus Athena, or Redshift Ignoring DynamoDB throttling because retries succeed Latency degrades until it becomes an outage Alarm on throttling; check key distribution Cache smaller than the working set Low hit rate, load pushed back to the database Monitor evictions and hit rate; resize

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
AWS rejects the idea that one database should serve every workload. Characterise the access pattern first, then choose the store.

Area Key lesson Managed databases AWS removes the heavy lifting; you still own schema, queries, indexes and access control Relational vs NoSQL ACID and flexible SQL with a single-writer ceiling, versus horizontal scale with access patterns fixed up front CAP and PACELC Partitions force C or A; in normal operation every read trades latency against consistency OLTP vs OLAP Keep analytics off the transactional database RDS / Aurora Default for relational data; Aurora adds shared six-copy storage and faster failover DynamoDB Serverless key-value at any scale; the partition key decides whether it scales ElastiCache Microsecond reads via cache-aside; never the system of record Replication vs standby vs backup Replicas scale reads, Multi-AZ provides availability, backups recover from mistakes

Next: with the data tier understood, 1.6 AWS Network Services covers the VPC, subnets and routing that these databases live inside.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: Networking Services: Amazon VPC, Amazon Route 53, and Amazon API Gateway
Definition
docs.text:
This topic covers the three services that decide how a request reaches your application:

Service What it is Scope Amazon VPC A logically isolated, software-defined network in which you place AWS resources, using an IP range you choose Regional: spans every AZ in one Region, never crosses Regions Amazon Route 53 A highly available authoritative DNS service, with domain registration, health checks and DNS-based traffic routing Global (control plane anchored in us-east-1) Amazon API Gateway A fully managed front door for APIs: authentication, validation, throttling, caching and monitoring without application code Regional

Route 53 turns a name such as api.example.com into an address. The VPC decides whether a packet can travel to that address. API Gateway is one of the managed entry points that sits in that path.

AWS network services

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Where networking sits in the architecture

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

The three layers of a network answer

Almost every AWS networking problem breaks into three layers. When something does not work, check them in this order:

  1. Name resolution (Route 53): what address do I connect to?
  2. Path (route tables, gateways, endpoints): can the packet get there?
  3. Permission (security groups, NACLs, IAM and resource policies): is the packet allowed?

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
Why Amazon VPC
docs.text:
The original EC2 network (EC2-Classic) put every customer on one flat shared network. There was no customer-defined address space, no subnets, no route tables and no private-only instances. Enterprises could not accept this:

  1. No network isolation. Regulated workloads need a database to be unreachable from the internet as a property of the network, not just of a firewall rule.
  2. No address planning. Connecting to an on-premises data centre over VPN or Direct Connect requires addresses that do not collide.
  3. No tiering. The classic three-tier design depends on saying "this subnet has no route to the internet".

Amazon VPC (launched 2009, the default since 2013) gave customers a network they could design. Compared with a data centre, a subnet is an API call rather than a VLAN change, the router is built in and free, and the firewall is enforced at every network interface rather than in a shared appliance.

docs.title: Why Route 53
docs.text:
Running authoritative DNS yourself is hard: it needs globally distributed infrastructure, DDoS resistance and near-perfect availability, because when DNS fails, everything fails.

Route 53 also turns DNS into a traffic-management tool. Classic DNS answers "what is the address of this name?" Route 53 can answer "what is the best address for this user, given health, latency, location and weighting?" That makes DNS a mechanism for global failover and gradual releases.

docs.title: Why API Gateway
docs.text: Before managed API front doors, every service re-implemented authentication, rate limiting, request validation, CORS and per-route metrics. This code was duplicated, drifted between services and caused many security incidents. API Gateway moves these concerns into a managed tier in front of your code. It also makes serverless HTTP possible: a Lambda function has no listening port, so something must terminate TLS and invoke it.

docs.title: The VPC as a software-defined network
docs.text: A VPC is not a physical network. Your instances share hosts and network fabric with other customers; isolation is enforced in software at every host. That is why you cannot sniff a neighbour's traffic, why broadcast and multicast do not work natively, and why a security group is not a chokepoint that can be overwhelmed.

docs.title: CIDR and Address Planning
docs.text:
CIDR notation writes a network as address/prefix-length. The prefix length is the number of fixed leading bits; the rest number the hosts. A /16 fixes 16 bits and leaves 16, giving 65,536 addresses. Each extra prefix bit halves the size.

CIDR Total addresses Usable in an AWS subnet Typical use /16 65,536 65,531 Largest VPC CIDR block /20 4,096 4,091 Common private application subnet /24 256 251 Public subnet for load balancers and NAT /26 64 59 Minimum practical subnet for an ALB /28 16 11 Smallest subnet AWS permits

VPC and subnet blocks must be between /16 and /28. A VPC can add secondary CIDR blocks later; this is the normal remedy when it runs out of addresses.

AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet. In 10.0.1.0/24 they are .0 (network address), .1 (VPC router), .2 (Amazon-provided DNS), .3 (future use) and .255 (broadcast, not supported but reserved).

The reserved-address trap

A /28 gives 11 usable addresses, not 16, and an ALB needs at least 8 free addresses per subnet to scale. Undersized subnets fail with InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet during a traffic spike, exactly when scaling matters most. Containers make this worse: ECS awsvpc mode and the EKS VPC CNI use one VPC IP per task or Pod.

A reference plan. Allocate hierarchically so ranges never collide across environments and Regions:

Scope CIDR Rationale Production, Region A 10.0.0.0/14 Room for several VPCs, summarisable in one route Production VPC 1 10.0.0.0/16 Public /24s, private /20s and isolated /22s per AZ (see Common configuration) Reserved for growth 10.0.128.0/17 Do not allocate the second half on day one Non-production / DR Region 10.4.0.0/14 / 10.8.0.0/14 Distinct ranges so peering stays possible

Overlapping CIDRs are effectively permanent

VPC peering and Transit Gateway cannot connect networks with overlapping CIDRs. A VPC's CIDR cannot be changed and subnets cannot be resized. If two teams both chose 10.0.0.0/16, the fix is rebuilding a VPC or inserting a NAT layer. Address planning is one of the few AWS decisions that is genuinely expensive to reverse.

docs.title: Subnets and Availability Zones
docs.text:
A subnet is a range of addresses inside a VPC, bound to exactly one Availability Zone. To survive the loss of an AZ you need subnets, and running capacity, in at least two AZs, preferably three.

What makes a subnet public or private is only its route table:

Subnet type Route table contains Typical contents Public A route to an Internet Gateway Load balancers, NAT gateways Private A default route to a NAT gateway (outbound only) Application instances, containers Isolated Neither Databases, caches

AZ names versus AZ IDs

The name us-east-1a maps to different physical zones in different accounts. The AZ ID (for example use1-az2) is the same everywhere. Compare AZ IDs when aligning resources across accounts, for example to avoid cross-AZ data charges.

docs.title: Route tables
docs.text:
Every VPC has a built-in router; route tables tell it where to send traffic. Each subnet uses exactly one route table; without an explicit association it uses the VPC's main route table.

  • Longest prefix match: the most specific matching route wins, regardless of order.
  • Every route table has a local route for the VPC CIDR. It cannot be removed and always handles traffic inside the VPC.
VPC packet routing

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Timeout versus connection refused

A packet with no matching route is silently dropped, and a security group or NACL denial is also silent. Both appear to the application as a timeout. A connection refused (TCP reset) means the packet arrived and the destination rejected it. Reading this difference is the most useful troubleshooting reflex in AWS networking.

docs.title: Internet Gateway
docs.text:
An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a highly available component attached to a VPC (one per VPC). It is the route-table target for internet traffic, and it performs one-to-one NAT between an instance's private address and its public IP or Elastic IP. The instance never sees its public address: ip addr inside it shows only the private one. An IGW is free and adds no bandwidth limit.

For IPv6, which needs no NAT, an egress-only Internet Gateway allows outbound connections and their replies while blocking inbound ones.

Internet access needs four things

An IGW alone is not enough. An instance also needs a public IP or Elastic IP, a route to the IGW, and security group and NACL rules that allow the traffic.

docs.title: NAT Gateway
docs.text:
A NAT gateway lets instances in private subnets start outbound connections (patches, image pulls, third-party APIs) while the internet cannot connect to them.

  • It lives in a public subnet and uses an Elastic IP.
  • It is zonal: it does not fail over across AZs. Deploy one per AZ, each zone's private route table pointing at its own NAT gateway.
  • It scales automatically from 5 Gbps up to 100 Gbps, and supports up to 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination. Exceeding that produces ErrorPortAllocation.
  • It cannot accept inbound connections, so it cannot publish a service.

The most common avoidable networking cost

NAT gateways charge per hour and per gigabyte processed. A workload that pulls images and writes to S3 through NAT can spend more on NAT than on compute. A Gateway endpoint for S3 is free and removes that traffic from the NAT path.

docs.title: Security Groups Versus Network ACLs
docs.text:
The two packet filters in a VPC. This fundamentals comparison is examined constantly.

Dimension Security group Network ACL Attaches to Network interfaces (instances, tasks, load balancers, RDS, endpoints) Subnets State Stateful: replies to allowed traffic are allowed automatically Stateless: replies need their own rule Rule types Allow only Allow and deny Evaluation All rules; any allow permits In rule-number order; first match wins Default New group: all outbound, no inbound Default NACL allows all; a custom NACL denies all until rules are added Source can be CIDR, prefix list, another security group CIDR only Typical use The main control; expresses application intent Coarse subnet guardrail; blocking a specific CIDR

The ephemeral-port trap

Because a NACL is stateless, the reply to an inbound HTTPS request goes to the client's ephemeral port, so outbound NACL rules must allow 1024-65535. Forgetting this makes every connection hang. Put the real policy in security groups and keep NACLs coarse.

Security group design, connection tracking and NACL incident use are covered in 8.2 Network Security and Network ACLs and VPC Flow Logs.

docs.title: Security Group Referencing  the Cloud-Native Idiom
docs.text:
A security group rule's source can be another security group instead of a CIDR. For example, sg-app allows TCP 8080 from sg-alb. As load balancer nodes scale and tasks are replaced with new IP addresses, the rule stays correct with no edits.

This is identity-based rather than address-based policy: a firewall rule that survives elasticity. CIDR-based rules in an auto-scaling environment drift and become a maintenance defect. 8.2 builds on this with one group per service role and chained tiers.

docs.title: VPC Endpoints
docs.text:
By default, a call from a private subnet to an AWS service such as S3 goes out through the NAT gateway to the service's public endpoint. VPC endpoints keep that traffic on the AWS private network and remove the NAT dependency.

Aspect Gateway endpoint Interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) Services S3 and DynamoDB only Most AWS services, plus partner and your own services Mechanism A route in the route table to a prefix list A network interface with a private IP in your subnet Reachable over peering, VPN, Direct Connect No Yes Security control Endpoint policy Endpoint policy plus a security group Cost Free Per hour per AZ, plus per gigabyte 
graph LR
    subgraph vpc["Amazon VPC"]
        subgraph priv["Private Subnet"]
            APP["Application instance or task"]
            ENI["Interface endpoint ENI"]
        end
        RT["Route table"]
    end
    APP -->|"Route to S3 prefix list"| RT
    RT --> GWE["Gateway endpoint"]
    GWE --> S3["Amazon S3"]
    APP -->|"Private DNS resolves to the ENI"| ENI
    ENI --> PL["AWS PrivateLink"]
    PL --> SM["Secrets Manager"]
    PL --> ECR["Amazon ECR"]

PrivateLink can also publish a service

A provider can put a Network Load Balancer in front of a service, create a VPC endpoint service, and let named accounts create Interface endpoints to it. Consumers reach it through an address in their own VPC: no peering, no route exchange, and no CIDR-overlap problem. This is the standard way to deliver SaaS privately.

docs.title: VPC Peering Versus Transit Gateway
docs.text:
VPC peering is a one-to-one private connection between two VPCs (same or different Region and account). It is non-transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C.

AWS Transit Gateway is a regional hub. Each VPC, VPN or Direct Connect gateway attaches once, and the hub routes between attachments. This turns an n(n−1)/2 mesh into n attachments.

graph TD
    subgraph mesh["VPC peering: full mesh"]
        A1["VPC A"] --- B1["VPC B"]
        A1 --- C1["VPC C"]
        B1 --- C1
    end
    subgraph hub["Transit Gateway: hub and spoke"]
        TGW["Transit Gateway"]
        TGW --- A2["VPC A"]
        TGW --- B2["VPC B"]
        TGW --- VPN["Site-to-Site VPN"]
        TGW --- DX["Direct Connect gateway"]
    end
Criterion VPC peering Transit Gateway Transitive routing No Yes Connections for n VPCs n(n−1)/2 n On-premises integration No Native (VPN, Direct Connect) Segmentation Implicit (which peerings exist) Explicit (multiple TGW route tables) Cost No hourly charge; data transfer applies Per attachment hour plus per gigabyte Choose when Two to about five VPCs, stable, cost-sensitive Many VPCs, hybrid connectivity, multi-account

Decision rule

Below roughly five VPCs with no on-premises link, peering is cheaper and simpler. Beyond that, or as soon as you need VPN, Direct Connect or segmentation, choose Transit Gateway.

docs.title: Load balancers and CloudFront in the request path
docs.text:
These services are covered elsewhere; here, only their place in the path matters.

  • Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic across targets in several AZs. Its nodes live in the subnets you choose and their addresses change, so always use the load balancer's DNS name or a Route 53 alias, never an IP. An ALB works at layer 7 (HTTP routing by host and path); an NLB works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP, static IP per AZ, very high throughput). Load balancers are used hands-on with ECS in Unit 2.
  • Amazon CloudFront terminates TLS at the edge location nearest the user, serves cached content, and forwards misses over the AWS backbone. It helps dynamic APIs too, by shortening the TLS handshake distance. The edge network is introduced in 1.1.

docs.title: DNS fundamentals and Route 53
docs.text:
DNS is a distributed, hierarchical, cached database: resolution goes from the root, to the top-level domain, to the zone's authoritative name servers.

Concept Meaning Public / private hosted zone Answers the internet / answers only the VPCs associated with it Split-horizon DNS The same name in a public and a private zone, resolving differently inside and outside the VPC NS records Delegate authority; Route 53 gives each public zone four name servers, which you set at the registrar TTL How long resolvers may cache an answer. Short (about 60 s) speeds failover; long (300 to 3600 s) reduces cost and suits stable records Health check Active probe of an endpoint, a CloudWatch alarm, or a combination of other checks Route 53 Resolver The DNS resolver inside every VPC (base address plus two); Resolver endpoints forward DNS to and from on-premises networks

Common record types.

Record Maps Note A / AAAA Name to IPv4 / IPv6 address The basic answer CNAME Name to another name Not allowed at the zone apex (example.com) Alias Name to an AWS resource Allowed at the apex; returns an A/AAAA answer; follows changing addresses; queries to AWS resources are free MX, TXT Mail servers; arbitrary text TXT is often used for domain verification NS, SOA Delegation; zone metadata Created automatically with the zone

Health checks cannot see private resources

Route 53 health checkers run on the public internet and cannot probe a private subnet. To fail over on a private resource's health, publish a CloudWatch metric and use a CloudWatch alarm health check.

docs.title: Route 53 routing policies
docs.text:
Policy What it does Typical use Caution Simple Returns one record (multiple values in random order) A single endpoint No health checks, no failover Weighted Splits answers by weight (0 to 255) Canary and blue-green releases, migration Caching makes the split approximate Latency Returns the Region with lowest latency to the resolver Multi-Region active-active Optimises speed, not compliance Failover Primary while healthy, otherwise secondary Active-passive disaster recovery Speed limited by TTL plus detection time Geolocation Answers by the user's continent or country Data residency, licensing, localisation Always add a default record Geoproximity Routes by distance, adjustable with a bias Gradually shifting traffic between Regions Needs Traffic Flow; harder to reason about Multivalue answer Up to eight healthy records at random Simple health-aware spreading Not a load balancer IP-based Answers by client CIDR ranges you define Steering specific networks or ISPs CIDR data must be maintained

Choosing a routing policy

Performance for global users: latency. Percentages or canaries: weighted. Legal or country rules: geolocation. Active-passive DR: failover.

DNS failover is coarse

Failover depends on TTL, and some resolvers ignore TTL. For faster failover, use a load balancer within a Region or AWS Global Accelerator across Regions, which shifts traffic at the network layer without relying on DNS caches.

docs.title: Amazon VPC
docs.text:
Architecture. A regional VPC contains zonal subnets. A built-in router follows per-subnet route tables. Gateways and endpoints are the exits. Filtering is enforced at every network interface.

Useful features beyond the basics. Flow Logs (metadata of accepted and rejected flows), prefix lists (named CIDR sets reusable in routes and rules), VPC sharing through Resource Access Manager (a network team owns the VPC; application accounts deploy into it), Reachability Analyzer (tells you from configuration whether A can reach B, and what blocks it), and AWS Network Firewall for egress filtering (8.2).

Pricing. The VPC, subnets, route tables, Internet Gateways, security groups and NACLs are free. You pay for NAT gateways, Interface endpoints, Transit Gateway, data transfer, and every public IPv4 address (hourly since 2024, attached or idle). See the cost table.

Availability. The router and Internet Gateways are highly available by design. NAT gateways, Interface endpoint interfaces and subnets are zonal: here your design, not AWS, decides availability.

Limits worth knowing. A VPC cannot span Regions. Its CIDR cannot change (only secondary blocks can be added) and subnets cannot be resized. Default quotas include 5 VPCs per Region and 5 security groups per network interface; most are adjustable in Service Quotas.

Common configuration. A /16 VPC across three AZs: one public /24 per AZ for load balancers and NAT, one private /20 per AZ for compute, one isolated /22 per AZ for data, one NAT gateway per AZ, Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, Interface endpoints for the AWS APIs you call often, and Flow Logs enabled.

docs.title: Amazon Route 53
docs.text:
Architecture and features. Globally distributed name servers, a global health-checker fleet and a Resolver in every VPC. Features: Public and private hosted zones (split-horizon), alias records, the routing policies above, health checks, Traffic Flow (a visual editor for combining policies), Resolver endpoints for hybrid DNS, Resolver DNS Firewall, and DNSSEC signing.

Availability. Route 53 offers a 100 percent availability SLA for its DNS data plane, unique among AWS services.

Pricing. Per hosted zone per month, per million queries (rates vary by policy), and per health check per month. Alias queries to AWS resources are free.

Propagation. Record changes reach all Route 53 name servers within about 60 seconds, but what users see depends on TTL and resolver caching.

docs.title: Amazon API Gateway
docs.text:
API Gateway is the managed front door between clients and backend compute (Lambda, ECS, EKS, EC2 or any HTTP endpoint). This section is an introduction; the full treatment of features, throttling levels, usage plans and pricing is in 4.2 API Management and Service Mesh.

Core vocabulary.

Term Meaning Integration What API Gateway calls: Lambda, an HTTP endpoint, an AWS service directly, or a private resource through a VPC Link Stage A named deployment (dev, prod) with its own settings, throttling and URL Authorizer IAM, Amazon Cognito, a Lambda authorizer, or (HTTP APIs) a built-in JWT authorizer Throttling Token-bucket rate and burst limits that protect the backend

The three API types.

Dimension REST API HTTP API WebSocket API Model Request-response Request-response Persistent two-way connection Relative cost Highest Roughly 70 percent cheaper than REST Per message and connection minute Endpoint types Edge, Regional, Private Regional Regional WAF, API keys and usage plans, caching, request validation Yes No No Best for Regulated or monetised APIs Most new serverless APIs Chat, live dashboards, notifications

Choosing the API type

Start with an HTTP API. Move to a REST API only for a feature it alone offers (WAF, API keys, request validation, caching, private or edge endpoints). Use a WebSocket API only when the server must push to the client. The type cannot be changed after creation.

Direct service integration

API Gateway can put a message on SQS or start a Step Functions execution with no Lambda function in between. When an API only needs to accept and enqueue work, this removes a whole compute tier.

Limits that shape design. By default: 10,000 requests per second with a 5,000-request burst per account per Region; a 29-second default integration timeout; a 10 MB payload limit (use pre-signed S3 URLs for large uploads). Long-running work should be made asynchronous. API Gateway will accept more traffic than your backend can serve, so per-route throttling is a design tool.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text:
The components a request meets, in order, and what each is responsible for:

Component Responsibility Scope Route 53 Resolves the name; applies routing policy and health checks Global CloudFront (optional) Terminates TLS near the user; caches Edge API Gateway / ALB / NLB Entry point: authentication and throttling, or HTTP / TCP load balancing Regional, multi-AZ VPC Address space and network boundary Regional Subnet + route table Address range in one AZ; decides where traffic goes Zonal Internet Gateway / NAT gateway Internet path in and out / outbound only VPC / zonal Security group / NACL Permits traffic at the interface / subnet Interface / subnet VPC endpoints Private path to AWS services Route table / zonal Peering / Transit Gateway Connects VPCs and on-premises networks VPC pair / regional Compute and data (EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda, RDS) The workload that finally handles the request Placement decides resilience

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning VPC Logically isolated virtual network in one Region CIDR block IP range written as address/prefix, for example 10.0.0.0/16 Subnet A CIDR range inside a VPC, in exactly one AZ Public / private / isolated subnet Route to an IGW / route to a NAT gateway / neither Route table Routes applied to traffic leaving a subnet Internet Gateway Internet path plus one-to-one NAT for public addresses NAT gateway Zonal, managed outbound-only internet access for private subnets ENI Elastic network interface; carries addresses and security groups Security group Stateful, allow-only filter on network interfaces Network ACL Stateless, ordered allow and deny filter on subnets Ephemeral port Short-lived client port, typically 1024 to 65535 Gateway endpoint Free route-based private path to S3 or DynamoDB Interface endpoint Network interface giving a private path to a service via PrivateLink VPC peering Non-transitive private link between two VPCs Transit Gateway Regional hub with transitive routing between VPCs, VPN and Direct Connect VPC Flow Logs Metadata records of accepted and rejected flows Hosted zone Container of DNS records for a domain; public or private Alias record Route 53 record pointing at an AWS resource; usable at the apex TTL How long a resolver may cache a DNS answer VPC Link API Gateway connection to private resources in a VPC

docs.title: VPC configuration
docs.text: Setting Guidance VPC CIDR /16 unless there is a strong reason; unused space is free DNS support and DNS hostnames Enable both; Interface endpoint private DNS needs them Auto-assign public IPv4 Off for private and isolated subnets Route table association Always explicit; relying on the main route table causes accidents IPv6 Consider dual stack to reduce public IPv4 charges Interface endpoint private DNS Enable so existing code needs no change Endpoint policy Restrict to your own buckets and accounts to prevent data exfiltration

docs.title: API Gateway Configuration
docs.text:
Only the settings that affect network design. Authorizer, throttling and logging settings are covered in 4.2.

Setting Options Guidance Endpoint type Edge-optimised, Regional, Private Regional plus your own CloudFront gives most control; Private for internal APIs Integration Lambda proxy, HTTP proxy, AWS service, VPC Link Prefer proxy integrations; VPC Link to reach a private ALB or NLB Caching Off, or a sized cache per stage (REST only) Charged per hour; justify with a measured hit rate CORS Per API or per route Configure at the gateway, not in every handler

docs.title: Design Considerations
docs.text:
Entry-point decision framework

Image Source: AI Generated (Chatgpt)

Quality What to design for Scalability The fabric scales itself; address space, NAT capacity and downstream capacity do not. EKS is the usual cause of IP exhaustion: 300 nodes with 30 Pods each need about 9,000 addresses. Bound API Gateway with throttling so scaling does not just move the failure to the database Availability List the zonal components and make each loss survivable: one NAT gateway per AZ, Interface endpoints in every AZ used, load balancers in at least two (preferably three) subnets, Multi-AZ RDS, Route 53 failover records Latency Every hop adds latency and a failure mode. Terminate TLS at the edge, reuse connections, remove components that exist only by habit Cost Charges are per gigabyte and invisible in code: NAT processing, cross-AZ traffic, internet egress, endpoint hours, public IPv4 Maintainability Prefer fewer parts; reference security groups instead of CIDRs; define everything in code

The single NAT gateway anti-pattern

Routing every private subnet to one NAT gateway saves one hourly charge but causes two problems. If that AZ fails, every private subnet loses outbound access, so a zonal failure becomes a VPC-wide failure. And traffic from other AZs pays cross-AZ charges on top of NAT processing.

docs.title: AWS Best Practices
docs.text: Pillar Network-specific practice Operational Excellence Define the network in code (5.3), in a stack separate from applications; tag every resource; check paths with Reachability Analyzer Security Private by default; security groups reference security groups; restrict endpoint policies; enable Flow Logs Reliability Three AZs where available (two minimum); one NAT gateway per AZ; recovery that does not depend on control-plane calls in the failed Region Performance Efficiency CloudFront in front of user-facing traffic; Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; connection reuse Cost Optimization Audit NAT traffic and move top talkers to endpoints; release idle Elastic IPs; prefer HTTP APIs Sustainability Less data moved means less energy: cache at the edge, compress, remove unnecessary hops

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Defence in depth applied to the network

Image Source: AI Generated (Chatgpt)

  • Nothing public by default. Only load balancers and NAT gateways belong in public subnets.
  • No open SSH. Port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 is the most common finding in AWS security reviews. Use Systems Manager Session Manager, which needs no inbound port and no bastion host.
  • Network permissions are dangerous IAM permissions. ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress can open a database to the world; keep it out of application deployment roles (8.1).
  • Keep service calls private. Reach Secrets Manager, KMS and S3 through endpoints, and use the aws:SourceVpce condition so leaked credentials do not work outside your network (8.3).
  • Encrypt in transit. Terminate TLS at CloudFront or the load balancer with ACM certificates; CloudFront certificates must be in us-east-1.
  • Log everything. Flow Logs, CloudTrail, Resolver query logs and access logs answer who did what and which flows were rejected.

WAF, Shield and detailed security group and NACL design are covered in 8.2.

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Performance.

  • Cache at CloudFront (design the cache key; forwarding every header destroys the hit rate) and, for REST APIs, at the API Gateway stage. DNS TTL is also a cache.
  • Reuse connections at every layer: HTTP keep-alive, database pools, SDK clients created outside the Lambda handler.
  • Lambda in a VPC gets no internet access unless its subnet routes to a NAT gateway; attach a function to a VPC only when it must reach a private resource (see 1.3).

Cost.

Cost driver How to control it NAT gateway processing Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; Interface endpoints for ECR, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager NAT gateway hours One per AZ in production; fewer in development only Cross-AZ data transfer Keep chatty traffic within an AZ where availability allows Internet egress CloudFront and compression Public IPv4 addresses Remove unnecessary public IPs; release idle Elastic IPs; consider IPv6 Interface endpoints Create only for services called at volume; share centrally in large estates Transit Gateway Justify against peering below about five VPCs

A real cost investigation

A team's NAT data-processing charge exceeded its whole ECS compute bill. Flow Logs analysed in Athena showed 78 percent of NAT bytes went to S3 and Amazon ECR. A free S3 Gateway endpoint plus Interface endpoints for ecr.api, ecr.dkr and logs cut the NAT charge by more than 80 percent. You cannot optimise what you have not measured.

Monitoring.

Signal Source Tells you Accepted and rejected flows VPC Flow Logs (metadata, not payloads) Misconfigurations, probes, what crosses the NAT gateway ErrorPortAllocation, BytesOutToDestination NAT gateway metrics Port exhaustion; cost driver Latency versus IntegrationLatency API Gateway metrics The gap is API Gateway's own overhead HealthCheckStatus Route 53 Failover readiness Security group and route changes CloudTrail Who changed what; alert on rules opening 0.0.0.0/0

Flow Log fields and security use are in 8.2; CloudWatch and X-Ray are covered in 7.1.

docs.title: Integration with Other AWS Services
docs.text: Service Network integration ECS awsvpc mode gives each task its own interface, IP and security groups (2.2) EKS VPC CNI gives each Pod a VPC IP, so subnets must be sized for Pod count (3.1) Lambda Optional VPC attachment for private resources (1.3) S3, DynamoDB Gateway endpoints; aws:SourceVpce in bucket policies RDS, ElastiCache Subnet groups across AZs; security group referencing the app's group (6.2) SQS, SNS, EventBridge Interface endpoints; direct API Gateway integration (6.3) CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform The network defined as code (Unit 5)

docs.title: Common Architecture Patterns
docs.text:
Three-tier web application. Internet-facing ALB in public subnets, an Auto Scaling group or ECS service in private subnets, Multi-AZ RDS in isolated subnets, a Route 53 alias to the ALB, and CloudFront in front. This remains the right default for many workloads.

Serverless API. Route 53 alias to an API Gateway custom domain, an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, Lambda proxy integration, and DynamoDB. If the functions need no private resources, the compute tier may need no VPC at all.

Private microservices. ECS services in awsvpc mode behind an internal ALB, discovered through private DNS, exposed externally only through API Gateway with a VPC Link. Each service has its own security group, so policy reads like the architecture diagram: "orders may call payments on port 8443".

Hub-and-spoke multi-account network. A network account owns a Transit Gateway shared through Resource Access Manager. Workload VPCs attach to it, an inspection VPC filters traffic, and a shared-services VPC hosts central endpoints so many accounts share one set.

Hub-and-spoke multi-account network

Image Source: AI Generated (Chatgpt)

Centralised egress. Instead of NAT gateways in every VPC, send internet-bound traffic through the Transit Gateway to one egress VPC. This saves NAT hours at scale but adds Transit Gateway processing charges and a hop; model the crossover.

Network-level releases use weighted Route 53 records, weighted ALB target groups or API Gateway canary stages (5.2). Retries, circuit breakers and bulkheads are covered in 4.3; event-driven decoupling in 1.7.

docs.title: Industry Use Cases
docs.text: Industry Requirement Networking design Banking Isolation and auditability Isolated data subnets, Interface endpoints for all AWS APIs, central Flow Logs Healthcare Hybrid, data residency Direct Connect plus Transit Gateway, geolocation routing IoT Devices pin IP addresses NLB with an Elastic IP per AZ SaaS Private delivery into customer VPCs PrivateLink endpoint services behind an NLB

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Isolation with software speed. Data-centre topology provisioned by API call.
  • No firewall chokepoint. Security groups are enforced at each network interface and scale with the fleet.
  • Identity-based rules. Security group referencing survives auto scaling and IP churn.
  • Private access to managed services. Endpoints and PrivateLink remove the internet path.
  • DNS as traffic control. Failover, canaries and compliance routing without code changes.
  • Shared API concerns handled once, in API Gateway rather than every service.
  • Everything is code. The network can be reviewed, reproduced and rebuilt.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Address planning is close to irreversible. CIDRs cannot change and subnets cannot be resized.
  • Peering is non-transitive and forbids overlap.
  • Zonal components are hidden single points of failure (NAT gateways, single-AZ endpoints).
  • Data transfer charges are invisible to developers.
  • DNS failover is limited by caching.
  • API Gateway limits (timeout, payload) force asynchronous designs for long or large operations; HTTP APIs lack some REST features, and the type cannot be changed.
  • Multi-account designs grow complex and need documentation and automated checks.

docs.title: Beginner Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it is wrong Do instead Calling a subnet public because of its name Only an IGW route makes it public Check the route table Instance in a public subnet with no public IP The IGW has nothing to translate to Assign a public or Elastic IP, or use a load balancer Application policy in NACLs Stateless rules break ephemeral-port replies Security groups for policy, NACLs as guardrails Sizing subnets by instance count Reserved addresses, ALB and container IPs are forgotten Size for peak tasks or Pods plus headroom Hard-coding a load balancer IP Its addresses change Use its DNS name or an alias record Overlapping CIDRs across environments Peering becomes impossible Plan ranges centrally

docs.title: Production Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Remedy One NAT gateway for the VPC Zonal failure becomes VPC-wide; cross-AZ charges One per AZ No S3 Gateway endpoint NAT processing charges on object traffic Add the free endpoint Security groups built from CIDR lists Rules drift as the fleet changes Reference security groups No Flow Logs Cost and incident analysis become guesswork Enable and centralise them Interface endpoints in one AZ A "private" design depends on one zone Create in every AZ used DR plans needing control-plane calls in the failed Region Recovery fails when needed Pre-provision and use health-check failover

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
AWS networking is about controlling three things deliberately: what a name resolves to (Route 53), where a packet may travel (VPC routing and endpoints), and who may send it (security groups, NACLs, API Gateway authorisers).

Area Key lesson VPC model A VPC is software, not wire: enforcement at every interface, no chokepoint, no broadcast Address planning The decision you cannot cheaply undo. Plan hierarchically, leave headroom, never overlap, allow for containers Subnets Public, private or isolated is decided only by the route table. One subnet = one AZ Filters Security groups are stateful and can reference each other, so they carry the real policy; NACLs are stateless guardrails Zonal components NAT gateways, Interface endpoints and subnets are per AZ; you make them highly available Endpoints Keeping traffic on the AWS network improves security and cuts NAT cost; the S3 Gateway endpoint is free Connectivity Peering for a few VPCs; Transit Gateway for many, hybrid or segmented networks Route 53 DNS as traffic control: alias records, routing policies and health checks, always limited by TTL API Gateway Managed front door; start with an HTTP API, choose REST only for its extra features

Next: with the network foundation in place, 1.7 Cloud-Native Design Patterns surveys the architecture patterns built on top of it.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: Cloud-Native Design Patterns: Serverless, Microservices, Event-Driven, API-First
Definition
docs.text:
A cloud-native design pattern is a reusable solution to a recurring architectural problem. It assumes the application runs on elastic, distributed, API-driven cloud infrastructure, not on fixed on-premises servers.

Cloud-native applications are designed for the cloud, not merely moved to it. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) describes cloud-native systems as loosely coupled, resilient, manageable and observable, combined with robust automation so that engineers can make high-impact changes frequently and predictably.

Four patterns form the structural pillars of cloud-native design:

Pattern One-sentence definition Question it answers Serverless Run code without provisioning or managing servers; the provider allocates compute on demand and bills per use How is compute provisioned and billed? Microservices Split an application into small, independently deployable services, each owning its data How is the system decomposed? Event-Driven Components communicate by producing and consuming events asynchronously How do parts communicate without coupling? API-First Design and agree the API contract before writing implementation code How is integration governed?

Patterns, not products

A pattern is a way of thinking; a service is a tool. You can build microservices badly on EKS, and you can build a serverless system that breaks every microservices principle. Examinations and interviews test whether you understand the pattern, not whether you can name the service.

docs.title: The problem with the traditional monolith
docs.text:
The traditional enterprise application was a monolith on long-lived servers:

  • All features in one deployable artifact and one shared relational database.
  • Scaling meant a bigger server, or cloning the whole application even if only one feature was busy.
  • One bug could crash everything; one deployment risked every feature.
  • Releases took weeks or months because every team coordinated around one artifact.
  • Capacity was bought for peak load, so servers sat mostly idle but were paid for 24/7.

docs.title: Why the cloud demanded new patterns
docs.text:
Cloud infrastructure changed three assumptions:

  1. Compute became elastic and metered. Provisioning for peak is wasteful when capacity arrives in seconds and is billed per second. Serverless takes this to its conclusion: pay per invocation.
  2. Failure became normal. In a fleet of thousands of machines across Availability Zones, something is always failing. Architectures must isolate failure (microservices) and absorb it asynchronously (event-driven).
  3. Delivery speed became a competitive advantage. Independent deployability (microservices) and stable contracts (API-first) make frequent deployment safe.
Dimension Traditional monolith Cloud-native Deployment unit One large artifact Many small services or functions Scaling Vertical, whole application Horizontal, per component, automatic Failure blast radius Entire application One service or function Data ownership One shared database Database per service Communication In-process method calls Network calls: APIs and events Capacity model Provision for peak Elastic, pay per use Release cadence Weeks to months Minutes to hours Team structure Layered (UI team, DB team) Cross-functional, service-aligned Evolution of software architecture stages

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Conway's Law

Organisations design systems that mirror their communication structures. Microservices are as much an organisational pattern as a technical one: small autonomous teams own small autonomous services. Amazon's "two-pizza team" rule is the organisational twin of the microservices pattern.

docs.title: Coupling and cohesion
docs.text:
These two ideas underlie all four patterns.

  • Coupling is how much components depend on each other. Cloud-native design reduces three kinds:
    • Technology coupling: a service should not care what language or database another service uses.
    • Temporal coupling: a producer should not need the consumer to be available right now. Event-driven design removes this.
    • Location coupling: a producer should not need to know who or how many consumers exist.
  • Cohesion is how well the responsibilities inside one component belong together. A good microservice has high cohesion: it does one business capability completely.

One rule to remember

Aim for low coupling between components and high cohesion within them. Every pattern below is a way of achieving that.

docs.title: Serverless  core concepts
docs.text:
• Function as a Service (FaaS): code packaged as functions triggered by events. AWS Lambda is the canonical FaaS.
  • Serverless is broader than FaaS: S3, DynamoDB on-demand, SQS, EventBridge, Fargate, Aurora Serverless and Step Functions are also serverless, because you never manage capacity.
  • Scale-to-zero: no traffic means no compute cost. This is the defining economic property.
  • Stateless, short-lived environments: state must live in external stores such as DynamoDB, S3 or ElastiCache.
  • Cold start: the extra latency of creating a new execution environment when no warm one is free. It is the price of scale-to-zero.
  • Concurrency model: Lambda handles one request per environment and scales by adding environments, not threads.
Lambda invocation: warm start versus cold start

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

How Lambda works internally (execution environments, memory and CPU, concurrency, Provisioned Concurrency and SnapStart) is covered in 1.3 AWS Compute Services.

docs.title: Microservices  core concepts
docs.text:
• Bounded context (from Domain-Driven Design): each service maps to one business subdomain with its own vocabulary, such as Orders, Inventory or Payments.
  • Independent deployability: the single most important test. If deploying service A needs service B's team, you have a distributed monolith.
  • Database per service: each service owns its data and exposes it only through its API or events.
  • Smart endpoints, dumb pipes: business logic lives in services; the network (ALB, SQS) only transports messages.
  • Service discovery: services find each other through DNS (AWS Cloud Map), load balancers or a service mesh, not hard-coded addresses.
  • Decentralised governance: teams choose their own languages and databases within organisational guardrails.

On AWS a containerised microservice is built into an image (ECR), scheduled by ECS or EKS across Availability Zones, registered behind a load balancer or in Cloud Map, and scaled on metrics. See 2.2 Amazon ECS, 2.3 and 3.1 Amazon EKS Architecture for how the orchestrators do this, and 4.1 Microservices Design Principles for decomposition, granularity and data ownership in depth.

The distributed monolith

The most common and most damaging failure mode: services are split physically but stay logically coupled. They share a database, must be released together, and call each other synchronously in long chains. This brings every cost of microservices and none of the benefits. Diagnostic question: can this service be deployed to production right now without coordinating with any other team? If not, it is not a microservice.

docs.title: Event-driven  core concepts
docs.text:
• Event: an immutable record that something happened, such as OrderPlaced or PaymentCaptured. Events are facts about the past, not requests.
  • Command versus event: a command (ChargeCard) asks one specific recipient to act and implies coupling; an event announces a fact to whoever cares.
  • Producer and consumer: producers emit events without knowing the consumers; consumers subscribe without knowing the producers.
  • Event router or broker: the intermediary, for example EventBridge, SNS, SQS or Kinesis.
  • Choreography versus orchestration:
    • Choreography: services react to each other's events with no central coordinator. Flexible, but the overall flow is implicit.
    • Orchestration: a central coordinator (Step Functions) directs the workflow. Visible and auditable, but a central dependency.
  • Delivery semantics: at-least-once delivery is the practical default, so consumers must be idempotent (safe to process the same event twice).
  • Eventual consistency: consumers process events after the fact, so services' views of the data converge over time rather than instantly.

Each broker implements a different messaging model. The model, not the brand name, is what the pattern depends on:

Broker Model What happens to a message after it is read SQS Point-to-point queue; consumers poll Hidden while processed, deleted on success, retried if not; repeated failures go to a dead-letter queue SNS Pub/sub topic; the service pushes A copy goes to every subscription EventBridge Event bus; rules match on event content Delivered to the targets of every matching rule; can be archived and replayed Kinesis Data Streams Ordered, partitioned log Kept for the retention period; each consumer tracks its own position and can replay Event-driven architecture example

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Service mechanics (visibility timeout, FIFO, DLQ redrive, filters, shards, rules, archives and Pipes) are covered in 6.3 Messaging and Event Streaming: see SQS, SNS, Kinesis and EventBridge.

At-least-once means duplicates will happen

SQS standard queues, SNS and EventBridge all deliver at least once. Retries and timeouts produce duplicates in production. Make consumers idempotent, for example by recording processed event IDs in DynamoDB with a conditional write. See 4.3 Idempotency.

docs.title: API-first  core concepts
docs.text:
• Contract-first design: the specification (OpenAPI for REST, a GraphQL schema, AsyncAPI or EventBridge schemas for events) is written, reviewed and agreed before implementation.
  • API as product: APIs have consumers, documentation, versioning, SLAs and a lifecycle. They are products, not by-products.
  • Consumer-driven design: the contract is shaped by what consumers need, not by the internal data model.
  • Versioning and backward compatibility: contracts evolve additively; breaking changes need a new version and a deprecation timeline.
