docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) is a managed Kubernetes service. It lets an organisation run Kubernetes clusters on AWS without operating the Kubernetes control plane itself.

Every Kubernetes cluster has two halves:

  • Control plane: manages the cluster and exposes the Kubernetes API.
  • Data plane: the compute on which application Pods run.

In EKS, AWS runs the control plane in an AWS-managed account. The data plane runs inside your VPC, on compute you choose. The defining fact of EKS is therefore a boundary through the middle of the cluster:

Side What runs there Who owns it Who pays Control plane kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, controller managers, IAM authenticator AWS, in an AWS-managed VPC Flat per-cluster hourly fee Data plane kubelet, kube-proxy, containerd, VPC CNI, CoreDNS, your Pods You, in your VPC, on EC2 or Fargate The compute, storage and network you use

How this unit flows

3.1 explains how an EKS cluster is built (control plane, networking, identity). 3.2 explains how applications are deployed onto it. 3.3 goes deeper into the data plane choices (Fargate, managed node groups, add-ons).

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
What Kubernetes does
docs.text:
Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform. Instead of starting containers by hand, you describe the desired state of an application, for example:

  • three replicas of a Pod;
  • a specific container image;
  • a fixed amount of CPU and memory;
  • a stable network address;
  • automatic replacement if a Pod fails.

Kubernetes repeatedly compares desired state with actual state and corrects any difference. This loop is called reconciliation, and it is the idea everything else in this unit builds on.

docs.title: Why a managed Kubernetes service
docs.text:
Running Kubernetes yourself means operating etcd, highly available API servers, control plane upgrades, and authentication. These are the hardest parts to run well, and a failure there makes the whole cluster unmanageable.

AWS runs the EKS control plane in its own account for three reasons:

  1. Isolation. Each control plane is single-tenant in its own VPC, so a mistake in your VPC cannot take it down.
  2. Operability. AWS can patch, scale and replace control plane instances without coordinating with you.
  3. An SLA. Because reliability does not depend on your VPC, AWS can offer an availability SLA on the API endpoint.

The cost of this design: the control plane sits outside your VPC but must reach inside it. EKS places cross-account network interfaces (ENIs) in your subnets for this path, and that path is the source of many real-world EKS problems.

docs.title: EKS or ECS?
docs.text:
Choose ECS when Choose EKS when The team has no Kubernetes experience The team already has, or will hire, Kubernetes skills The workload is AWS-only Multi-cloud, hybrid or on-premises portability is required You want the smallest operational surface You need the Kubernetes ecosystem: Helm charts, operators, service meshes Fast time to first deployment matters most You are building an internal platform for other teams

The decision is about the ecosystem, not the scheduler

Both orchestrators run containers well. If you need Kubernetes-packaged software, you need Kubernetes; if not, ECS reaches the same outcome with far fewer concepts (see 2.2 Amazon ECS). Kubernetes is not automatically "more advanced".

A control plane problem stops change, not traffic

Running Pods keep serving requests if the API server is briefly unavailable. What stops is the ability to deploy, scale or change anything.

docs.title: Nodes, Pods and containers
docs.text:
A node provides compute capacity. A Pod is the smallest Kubernetes workload unit: one or more containers sharing a network address and storage. Pods are scheduled onto nodes; they are not the same thing.

docs.text:
If you studied ECS in Unit 2, this mapping is the quickest way in:

ECS concept Kubernetes equivalent Key difference Task definition Pod spec (inside a Deployment) A Pod is a group of containers sharing one network namespace Task Pod Smallest schedulable unit Service Deployment + Service Kubernetes separates "keep N replicas running" from "give them a stable address" Cloud Map discovery Service + CoreDNS DNS is built in Container instance Node A Node is an API object with labels, taints and capacity Service auto scaling HorizontalPodAutoscaler Same control loop Task role ServiceAccount + Pod Identity or IRSA The largest conceptual gap (see IAM for workloads)

docs.title: How a request to the cluster flows
docs.text:
1. An engineer or pipeline submits desired state to the Kubernetes API.
  2. The control plane authenticates, authorises, validates and stores it in etcd.
  3. The scheduler picks a node for each new Pod.
  4. The kubelet on that node starts the containers.
  5. Controllers keep reconciling actual state with desired state.
  6. The VPC connects Pods to each other and to other AWS resources.
  7. IAM and Kubernetes RBAC decide what people and workloads may do.

docs.title: EKS control plane and worker nodes
The EKS control plane
docs.text:
Component Role On EKS kube-apiserver Front door: authenticates and authorises every request; the only component that talks to etcd At least two instances across AZs etcd Key-value store holding all cluster state Three instances across three AZs kube-scheduler Chooses a node for each unscheduled Pod AWS-managed kube-controller-manager Built-in reconciliation loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job) AWS-managed cloud-controller-manager AWS-specific loops such as node lifecycle AWS-managed AWS IAM Authenticator Verifies the IAM identity behind each kubectl request Built in

You operate the Kubernetes workloads; AWS operates the control plane infrastructure.

Key facts:

  • Availability. Components are spread across multiple Availability Zones and replaced automatically when unhealthy.
  • Pricing. A flat fee per cluster per hour (indicatively USD 0.10 per hour in standard support, about USD 0.60 in extended support), regardless of cluster size.
  • Scaling. AWS scales the control plane with load; there is no setting.
  • Limits. No direct etcd access. Upgrades go one minor version at a time and are effectively one-way. The VPC, control plane subnets and IP family are fixed at creation.

Upgrades are a yearly obligation

Each Kubernetes version gets about 14 months of standard support, then about 12 months of extended support at roughly six times the control plane price. Plan an annual upgrade (process covered in 3.2).

docs.title: Worker nodes: data plane options
docs.text:
Types of node

Image Source: AI Generated (Gemini)

Option You manage AWS manages Choose when Managed node group Instance types, scaling limits, labels AMI, bootstrap, health replacement, rolling upgrades The default for most clusters Self-managed nodes Everything about the nodes Only the control plane You need a custom AMI or unsupported setup AWS Fargate Nothing about infrastructure The whole node (one micro-VM per Pod) Small, bursty or isolation-sensitive Pods EKS Auto Mode Workloads and scaling policy Compute, networking, storage, load balancing You want AWS to run the data plane Hybrid Nodes On-premises hardware The control plane Workloads must stay on-premises

Fargate and managed node groups are compared in depth in 3.3.

A sensible first production cluster

Managed node groups in private subnets across three AZs, with VPC CNI, CoreDNS and kube-proxy managed as EKS add-ons. Add Fargate later for specific namespaces.

docs.title: How a node joins the cluster
docs.text:
A launched instance is not yet a node. It must authenticate to the API server and have working networking first.

Sequence diagram for a node joining the cluster

Image Source: AI Generated (Gemini)

Two practical consequences:

  1. A node stays NotReady until the VPC CNI works, so a broken CNI looks like nodes that never become ready.
  2. The node's IAM role needs an access entry. EKS creates it automatically for managed node groups; you create it yourself for self-managed nodes.

docs.title: EKS networking and VPC integration
docs.text: Nodes and Pods live in your VPC subnets. The VPC provides IP addresses, routing, security groups, internet access where allowed, and private connectivity through VPC endpoints.

docs.title: The Amazon VPC CNI
docs.text:
Many Kubernetes network plugins give Pods addresses from an internal overlay network. The Amazon VPC CNI is different: every Pod gets a real, routable IP address from your VPC subnet, taken from secondary IPs on the node's ENIs.

VPC CNI

Image Source: AI Generated (Chatgpt)

Benefit Cost No encapsulation overhead; one network to debug Pod density is limited by IP addresses, not just CPU and memory Pod traffic appears in VPC Flow Logs Each instance type supports a fixed number of ENIs and IPs Load balancers can target Pods directly Your subnet size becomes a cluster capacity limit

The most common EKS surprise

A cluster can run out of subnet IP addresses while nodes still have free CPU. New Pods then stay Pending. Size subnets for Pod count, not node count. (Prefix delegation, custom networking and IPv6 are ways around this; they are beyond this module.)

docs.title: Services, CoreDNS and kube-proxy
docs.text:
Pods are replaced often, so their IPs change. Other Pods reach them through a Service, which provides a stable name and virtual IP (ClusterIP).

  • CoreDNS resolves the Service name to its ClusterIP.
  • kube-proxy on each node rewrites packets for the ClusterIP so they reach a healthy Pod.
Services, CoreDNS, kube-proxy

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

Service type What it creates Use ClusterIP Internal virtual IP Default; service-to-service traffic NodePort A port on every node Rarely used directly LoadBalancer An AWS load balancer (NLB) Expose one Service externally Ingress (not a Service type) An ALB HTTP routing for many Services behind one load balancer

docs.title: The AWS Load Balancer Controller
docs.text:
This controller (installed by you) turns an Ingress into an ALB and an annotated Service into an NLB.

Target mode Traffic goes to Consequence Instance mode A node port, then kube-proxy forwards to a Pod Extra hop IP mode Pod IPs directly Lower latency; required on Fargate

docs.title: Cluster endpoint access
docs.text:
Mode Who can reach the API Typical use Public only Internet, limited by a CIDR allow-list Development Public and private Allow-listed internet plus the VPC; nodes stay internal Common production choice Private only Only from inside the VPC or a connected network Regulated environments

Plan the admin path before going private-only

With a private-only endpoint, every engineer and CI/CD pipeline must reach the cluster from inside the VPC (VPN, bastion, in-VPC runners). Teams that skip this lock themselves out.

docs.title: Subnets and Availability Zones
docs.text:
A common production layout:

  • private subnets for nodes and Pods;
  • public subnets for internet-facing load balancers;
  • NAT gateways for outbound internet from private subnets;
  • VPC endpoints for private access to AWS services such as ECR and S3.
Workload spread across Availability Zones

Image Source: AI Generated (Chatgpt)

The goal is not "many nodes" but surviving the loss of a whole AZ: spread both nodes and replicas across zones. Remember that cross-AZ traffic is billed.

docs.title: EKS security and IAM integration
docs.text:
EKS security has two separate questions:

  1. Who can operate the cluster? (people and pipelines using kubectl)
  2. What can the application in a Pod do in AWS? (workload identity)

docs.title: Cluster access: authentication versus authorisation
docs.text:
Step Layer Mechanism Failure message Authentication (who are you?) IAM kubectl sends a token from aws eks get-token Unauthorized Mapping EKS API An access entry links the IAM principal to a Kubernetes identity Unauthorized if missing Authorisation (what may you do?) Kubernetes An access policy (cluster admin, admin, edit, view) or RBAC Role binding Forbidden

Unauthorized vs Forbidden

Unauthorized means the cluster does not recognise you (no access entry). Forbidden means it recognises you but you lack permission. Only the identity that created the cluster has admin access by default, so add access entries for your team immediately.

docs.title: IAM for workloads: Pod identity
docs.text:
A Pod that writes to S3 needs AWS credentials. Three options:

Approach How it works Verdict Node instance role Every Pod on the node borrows the node's role Avoid: every Pod gets every permission IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) The cluster's OIDC provider lets a ServiceAccount assume an IAM role Works everywhere, including Fargate EKS Pod Identity An agent add-on supplies credentials for a ServiceAccount-to-role association Simpler; preferred on EC2 nodes; not on Fargate Pod access to other AWS services

Image Source: AI Generated (Chatgpt)

Both IRSA and Pod Identity give temporary, auto-rotated credentials, so no access key is stored in the container. Apply least privilege: each workload gets only what it needs.

Block Pods from the node role

Even with Pod Identity, a Pod can reach the node's role through the instance metadata service (IMDS). Require IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1 on nodes. You need both settings together.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Enable envelope encryption with AWS KMS for etcd, and use AWS Secrets Manager (with the Secrets Store CSI Driver) for credentials that rotate. Never delete the KMS key: every Secret would become unreadable.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text:
Component Responsibility EKS cluster Managed control plane: API endpoint, etcd, scheduler, controllers Cluster IAM role Role EKS uses to manage ENIs, load balancers and logs for you Cluster security group Lets the control plane and nodes talk to each other Cross-account ENIs The control plane's path into your VPC Cluster endpoint API server DNS name (public, public and private, or private) VPC and subnets At least two AZs; private for nodes, public for internet-facing load balancers Node IAM role Used by kubelet to join the cluster and pull images from ECR kubelet / containerd Node agent that runs Pods / container runtime VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy Pod IPs, cluster DNS, Service routing AWS Load Balancer Controller Creates ALBs for Ingress and NLBs for Services Access entries Map IAM principals to Kubernetes permissions Pod Identity Agent / OIDC provider Enable per-Pod IAM roles AWS KMS Envelope encryption of Secrets CloudWatch Logs and CloudTrail Control plane logs and audit of EKS API calls

Think of these in three groups:

  • Boundary components (endpoint, ENIs, security group, node role) decide whether the cluster works at all.
  • Data plane components (nodes, CNI, kube-proxy, CoreDNS) decide whether workloads run, and you keep them current.
  • Integration components (load balancer controller, Pod identity, KMS, CloudWatch) decide how much of AWS your Pods can use.

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Control plane Kubernetes management components AWS runs for you Data plane Nodes and Pods in your VPC that run workloads Pod Smallest schedulable unit; containers sharing a network address Node A machine (or Fargate capacity) that runs Pods kube-apiserver Front door to the cluster; only component that talks to etcd etcd Key-value store holding all cluster state kubelet Node agent that registers the node and runs Pods kube-proxy Implements Service virtual IPs on each node Reconciliation Continuous loop making actual state match desired state Standard / extended support About 14 months at base price / about 12 more months at a higher price Amazon VPC CNI Network plugin giving Pods real VPC IPs ENI Elastic network interface; Pod IPs are secondary addresses on it ClusterIP Internal virtual address of a Service Ingress HTTP routing object, realised on EKS as an ALB IP mode / instance mode Load balancer targets are Pod IPs / node ports Access entry EKS object mapping an IAM principal to a Kubernetes identity Access policy Managed permission set attached to an access entry RBAC Kubernetes authorisation: Roles, ClusterRoles and bindings ServiceAccount Kubernetes identity for a workload IRSA IAM Roles for Service Accounts, using OIDC federation EKS Pod Identity Newer per-Pod IAM mechanism using an agent add-on IMDSv2 hop limit Setting of 1 stops containers reaching the node's metadata service Envelope encryption KMS-backed encryption of Kubernetes Secrets NetworkPolicy Kubernetes rules controlling Pod-to-Pod traffic

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Setting Options Recommendation Kubernetes version Supported minor versions Stay in standard support Endpoint access Public, public and private, private Public and private with a CIDR allow-list Authentication mode CONFIG_MAP, API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, API API (access entries) for new clusters Secrets encryption None or a KMS key Enable; protect the key from deletion Control plane logging api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler At least audit and authenticator IP family IPv4 or IPv6 IPv4 unless there is a strong reason Subnets At least two AZs Three private subnets, sized for Pod count Compute model Node groups, Fargate, Auto Mode, self-managed Managed node groups as the baseline Workload identity Node role, IRSA, Pod Identity Pod Identity on EC2 nodes; IRSA on Fargate; never the node role Network policy None, VPC CNI native, Calico Enable; default-deny per namespace

Node group settings (capacity type, labels, taints) are covered in 3.3.

Some settings can never change

The IP family, VPC and control plane subnets are fixed at creation. Changing them means building a new cluster and migrating.

docs.title: Design Considerations
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Do we need Kubernetes, or would ECS do?"] -->|"ecosystem, portability"| B["EKS"]
    A -->|"simplest, AWS-only"| Z["ECS (Unit 2)"]
    B --> C{"How much of the data plane do we want to run?"}
    C -->|"as little as possible"| D["Auto Mode or Fargate"]
    C -->|"real nodes, little AMI work"| E["Managed node groups"]
    D --> G{"Is VPC address space adequate?"}
    E --> G
    G -->|"tight"| H["Plan larger subnets before creating the cluster"]
    G -->|"yes"| K{"How is the cluster administered?"}
    H --> K
    K -->|"from the internet"| L["Public and private endpoint with allow-list"]
    K -->|"regulated"| M["Private endpoint with VPN or bastion"]
    L --> N["Per-Pod IAM, IMDS hop limit 1, network policies"]
    M --> N
Quality Design levers Trade-off accepted Availability Three AZs, multiple replicas, PodDisruptionBudgets Higher cost; cross-AZ traffic Scalability Pod and node autoscaling, large enough subnets More moving parts Security Per-Pod IAM, private nodes, network policies, audit logs More operational friction Cost Right-sized requests, Spot, fewer shared clusters Shared clusters share blast radius Operability Managed node groups, EKS add-ons, Auto Mode Less control the more AWS manages

docs.title: Architecture scenarios
docs.text:
Scenario 1: University web application. Unpredictable traffic. Use managed node groups across three AZs, a Deployment with several replicas, an ALB via Ingress, RDS for data, and CloudWatch for observability. Kubernetes handles scheduling and recovery; managed AWS services hold state.

Scenario 2: Pod needs S3 access. Do not put an access key in the container. Create a ServiceAccount, associate it with a narrowly scoped IAM role through EKS Pod Identity, and grant only the required S3 actions. The application's identity is now separate from the node's.

docs.title: AWS Best Practices
docs.text: Pillar Practice Operational Excellence Define clusters and add-ons as code (5.3); enable control plane logging before you need it Security Access entries with least privilege; one IAM role per workload; IMDSv2 hop limit 1; private nodes; KMS for Secrets Reliability Three AZs; at least two replicas of important services; health probes and PDBs (see 3.2) Performance Efficiency IP-mode targets; instance types that fit workload and Pod density Cost Optimization Stay in standard support; avoid many small clusters; share one ALB via Ingress Sustainability Higher utilisation; consider Graviton instances

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Per-Pod identity + IMDS hop limit 1. Without both, a compromised Pod can use the node's IAM role.
  • Separate authentication from authorisation. Grant the narrowest access policy, scoped to a namespace; keep cluster-admin for a small break-glass role.
  • Admission control. Pod Security Admission blocks privileged Pods per namespace; Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper add organisational rules.
  • Network segmentation. NetworkPolicies for Pod-to-Pod rules; security groups for VPC boundaries such as database access.
  • Supply chain. Scan images in ECR, deploy by digest or immutable tag, keep node AMIs current.
  • Audit. CloudTrail records EKS API calls (clusters, node groups, access entries). Only the control plane audit log records Kubernetes API activity inside the cluster.

Deeper treatment: IAM in 8.1, network security in 8.2, KMS and Secrets Manager in 8.3.

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Performance. Use IP-mode targets to remove a hop. Keep images small so Pods start fast. Remember a node can run out of IPs before CPU.

Cost. The control plane fee is usually the smallest part of the bill.

Cost driver How to control it Control plane fee Stay in standard support; avoid unnecessary clusters Compute (EC2 or Fargate) Right-size requests; Spot above an On-Demand base (3.3) Load balancers Share one ALB across Services with Ingress NAT and data transfer VPC endpoints; watch cross-AZ traffic Logs and storage Set log retention; delete unused volumes Idle clusters Delete lab clusters when not in use

Monitoring.

Signal Source Tells you Node conditions (NotReady, MemoryPressure) kubectl get nodes, Container Insights Node health Pending Pods and events kubectl describe pod Why a Pod cannot be scheduled (CPU, memory, IPs) Free subnet IPs VPC / CloudWatch Early warning of IP exhaustion audit and authenticator logs CloudWatch Logs Who did what; why access was refused EKS API activity CloudTrail Changes to clusters, node groups, access entries

Observability is covered fully in Unit 7.

docs.title: Integration with Other AWS Services
docs.text:
Service Why it integrates with EKS Amazon EC2 Instances behind node groups Amazon VPC The network Pods live in Elastic Load Balancing ALBs for Ingress, NLBs for Services IAM and STS Cluster authentication and per-Pod roles Amazon ECR Image registry (2.1) EBS, EFS, S3 Persistent storage via CSI drivers (6.1) RDS, DynamoDB Managed databases (6.2) SQS, SNS, EventBridge Messaging with per-Pod roles (6.3) KMS and Secrets Manager Secrets encryption and injection CloudWatch and CloudTrail Logs, metrics, Container Insights, audit ACM and Route 53 TLS certificates and DNS for load balancers CodePipeline, CodeBuild, CloudFormation Delivery and infrastructure as code (Unit 5) Integration with other AWS services

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

The diagram shows three flows:

  • Delivery flow (commit → ECR → API server) changes what runs.
  • Runtime flow (Route 53 → ALB → Pod → AWS services) never touches the control plane, which is why apps survive a control plane problem.
  • Identity flow connects each Pod to its own IAM role.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• AWS runs the hardest part. etcd, API server availability and control plane patching, with a multi-AZ design and an SLA.
  • Upstream Kubernetes. Helm charts, operators and standard tools work unchanged.
  • Native VPC networking. Pods with real VPC IPs can be load balancer targets and appear in Flow Logs.
  • Fine-grained workload identity. Each Pod can have its own short-lived IAM role.
  • Auditable access. Access entries are visible in CloudTrail and definable as code.
  • Portability. Manifests run on any conformant Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Kubernetes is big. EKS does not shrink the concept count; first production deployment takes longer than on ECS.
  • "Managed" covers half the cluster. You still keep nodes, add-ons and controllers current.
  • Upgrades never stop. Roughly yearly, one minor version at a time, one-way.
  • IP planning is a hard limit. Out of subnet IPs means no new Pods.
  • Per-cluster fee pushes towards shared clusters and shared blast radius.
  • The control-plane-to-VPC path can break. Security group changes can stop webhooks, kubectl logs and kubectl exec.

docs.title: Beginner Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it is wrong Do instead "EKS manages everything" EKS manages the control plane; the data plane depends on your compute model Know which side each component is on "A node is a Pod" A node is capacity; a Pod is scheduled onto it Keep the terms distinct "IAM permission = Kubernetes permission" IAM authenticates; RBAC authorises; an access entry connects them Create an access entry and policy Creating the cluster with a pipeline role only Only the creator is admin Add a human admin access entry at once Putting app permissions on the node role Every Pod inherits them Pod Identity or IRSA per workload "Several nodes = high availability" Nodes in one AZ fail together Spread nodes and replicas across AZs Small subnets or tiny instance types Pods run out of IPs before CPU Size for Pod density Nodes in public subnets Data plane exposed Private subnets with NAT or endpoints

docs.title: Production Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Remedy Tightening the cluster security group blindly Deployments fail with webhook errors Allow control plane to node traffic; test after changes Falling into extended support Several times the control plane price Annual upgrade rehearsed in non-production Private-only endpoint with no access path Engineers and CI/CD locked out VPN, bastion or in-VPC runners first Not monitoring free IPs Scale-out fails without warning Alarm on free subnet addresses Deleting the Secrets KMS key All Secrets unreadable Protect the key from deletion

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Amazon EKS = Kubernetes orchestration + AWS-managed infrastructure. The central idea is the boundary through the cluster: AWS runs the control plane across multiple AZs in its own account; you choose and run the data plane in your VPC. A control plane problem stops change, not traffic.

Area Key lesson Control plane and nodes AWS runs API server, etcd, scheduler. Managed node groups are the default data plane; Fargate and Auto Mode hand more to AWS Networking VPC CNI gives each Pod a real VPC IP: great for load balancing, but IP space limits capacity. Spread across AZs Cluster access IAM authenticates, access entry maps, RBAC authorises. Unauthorized vs Forbidden Workload identity Pod Identity (EC2) or IRSA (Fargate), plus IMDS hop limit 1. Never the node role Operations Annual upgrades; cost is mostly compute, networking and logs, not the control plane fee

Next: with the cluster's architecture understood, 3.2 shows how to create a cluster and deploy applications onto it.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
3.1 explained how an EKS cluster is built. A cluster exists to run applications. Deploying an application on EKS means:

  1. describing the application's desired state as Kubernetes objects (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps);
  2. delivering those objects to the cluster's API server;
  3. letting the cluster's controllers make reality match them (reconciliation, see 3.1).

Deployment involves three separate concerns. Mixing them up causes most beginner confusion:

Concern Question it answers Typical tools Cluster provisioning Does a cluster exist with the right network, nodes, add-ons and access? eksctl, CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform, console Packaging Which objects describe this app, and how do they differ per environment? YAML manifests, Helm, Kustomize Delivery How do those objects reach the cluster repeatably? kubectl for learning, CI/CD pipelines for teams

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
docs.text:
• An image alone is not a running application. Something must decide how many copies run, where, how traffic reaches them, and what happens when one fails. Kubernetes objects describe that.
  • A usable cluster is more than one API call. It needs IAM roles, subnets, add-ons, nodes, access entries and a load balancer controller, created in the right order. Tools like eksctl understand this dependency graph.
  • Typing commands does not scale. Hand-run kubectl leaves no reviewed record and spreads cluster credentials. Teams store manifests in Git and deploy through pipelines. (GitOps tools such as Argo CD or Flux go further by pulling from Git; covered in later study.)
  • Environments differ. Dev, staging and production differ in replicas, sizes and image versions. Copying YAML per environment causes drift. Helm (parameterised packages) and Kustomize (base + overlays) solve this.

docs.title: Declarative deployment
docs.text: Kubernetes is declarative: you say what should be true ("three replicas of version 1.4.2"), not the steps to get there. To release a new version you change the description (the image tag) and apply it; Kubernetes performs the transition.

docs.title: The objects you write
docs.text:
Object Responsibility Container image Packages code and runtime ("what runs") Deployment Keeps N identical Pods running and manages updates ("how many, how updated") ReplicaSet Created by a Deployment for each version; holds the Pod count Service Stable network address in front of changing Pods Ingress External HTTP access, realised as an ALB (3.1) ConfigMap Non-secret configuration ServiceAccount Workload identity, linked to an IAM role (3.1) HorizontalPodAutoscaler Scales replica count from metrics PodDisruptionBudget Limits Pods evicted at once during maintenance (3.3) Namespace Logical grouping and isolation inside a cluster

Image vs Deployment

A container image is not a deployment strategy. The image answers what runs; the Deployment answers how many, how it is updated, and how it stays healthy.

docs.title: Creating and managing EKS clusters
docs.text:
Decisions at creation. Kubernetes version, Region, VPC and subnets (at least two AZs), endpoint access, authentication mode, compute model, IAM roles, add-ons, and logging. Most were explained in 3.1 Configuration Options.

Creating a cluster

Image Source: AI Generated (Google Gemini)

CreateCluster makes the control plane only

A brand-new cluster has an API server and no nodes. Only the identity that created it can log in until more access entries are added.

Build order, and what breaks if a stage is missing:

Stage What is created Symptom if skipped or wrong 1. Prerequisites Cluster role, node role, VPC, subnets, NAT Creation fails, or nodes cannot reach ECR 2. Control plane API server, etcd, cluster security group (10 to 15 min) Nothing else can proceed 3. Access Access entries for people and pipelines Unauthorized for everyone but the creator 4. Core add-ons VPC CNI, kube-proxy, CoreDNS Nodes never Ready; DNS fails 5. Node group Auto Scaling group and EC2 instances Every Pod stays Pending 6. Controllers AWS Load Balancer Controller, metrics-server Ingress does nothing; no autoscaling metrics

Subnets for load balancers need discovery tags: kubernetes.io/role/elb (public) and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb (private).

CoreDNS Pending on a new cluster is normal

With no nodes yet, CoreDNS has nowhere to run. It starts once a node group exists. Learning to tell "nowhere to run" from "broken" is a core Kubernetes skill.

Cluster lifecycle. Create → configure → deploy workloads → monitor → upgrade → maintain nodes → manage access → scale → delete.

Upgrading, at a high level. Versions are supported for a limited time (3.1), so upgrades are recurring. They go one minor version at a time in this order, because nodes may run behind the control plane but never ahead of it:

  1. Control plane (for example 1.30 → 1.31).
  2. Add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy) to versions matching the new control plane.
  3. Nodes, replaced with new ones via a rolling update (cordon, drain, PodDisruptionBudgets, see 3.3).

Before upgrading, check manifests for APIs removed in the target version, and rehearse in non-production first. Upgrades cannot be rolled back.

docs.title: Deploying applications using kubectl and eksctl
docs.text:
Tool Job AWS Console Visual management and learning AWS CLI AWS operations, including aws eks update-kubeconfig eksctl Create and manage EKS clusters and node groups kubectl Manage Kubernetes resources inside the cluster Helm Package and release Kubernetes applications

The critical distinction

eksctl builds the cluster (AWS side). kubectl manages what runs inside it (Kubernetes side). They are not interchangeable.

eksctl generates CloudFormation stacks for the cluster, VPC and node groups, and creates IAM roles, add-ons and access in the correct order.

For anything beyond a lab, put the definition in a ClusterConfig YAML file (eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml) so it is reviewable in Git. Production teams usually use their standard IaC tool instead (5.3).

Connecting kubectl to the cluster:

aws eks update-kubeconfig --name dso303-lab --region us-east-1
kubectl config current-context    # which cluster am I talking to?
kubectl get nodes                 # nodes should show STATUS Ready

This writes a context into ~/.kube/config: the endpoint, its certificate, and a command (aws eks get-token) that fetches a short-lived token before each request. No password is stored; your cluster identity is whichever AWS identity is active.

Check the context before every change

kubectl acts on the current context. The costliest Kubernetes mistakes are commands run against the wrong cluster. Give production contexts clearly different names.

Essential kubectl commands:

Command Purpose kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml Create or update objects from a file kubectl get pods -o wide List Pods with node and IP kubectl get deploy,svc List Deployments and Services kubectl describe pod <name> Detailed state and events: the most useful diagnostic kubectl logs <pod> --previous Output of the crashed container kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> Wait until a rollout really finishes kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> Return to the previous revision kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh Shell inside a running container kubectl port-forward svc/<name> 8080:80 Reach an internal Service from your machine

Use kubectl apply (create or update) rather than kubectl create (fails if the object exists).

kubectl describe pod first, always

Insufficient CPU, image pull failures, probe failures and out-of-memory kills all appear in plain English in the Pod's events. Read them before guessing.

Typical deployment workflow:

flowchart LR
    A["Build image"] --> B["Push to ECR with unique tag"]
    B --> C["Update image tag in manifest"]
    C --> D["kubectl apply / helm upgrade"]
    D --> E["Scheduler places Pods on nodes"]
    E --> F["Service + Ingress route traffic via ALB"]
    F --> G["kubectl rollout status"]
    G -->|"failed"| H["kubectl rollout undo"]

How a rolling update works. When the Pod template changes (for example a new image tag), the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and moves Pods across gradually:

  • maxSurge: how many extra Pods may exist during the update.
  • maxUnavailable: how many Pods may be missing.
  • New Pods get traffic only after their readiness probe passes. A broken version stalls the rollout while old Pods keep serving.

Kubernetes does not roll back automatically

A stalled rollout is marked failed after progressDeadlineSeconds, but nothing is reverted. Unlike the ECS deployment circuit breaker (2.3), you or your pipeline must run kubectl rollout undo. Also, kubectl apply returns when the object is stored, not when Pods are running, so always follow it with kubectl rollout status.

docs.title: Using Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts
Manifests
docs.text:
A manifest is a YAML file declaring Kubernetes objects. Stored in Git, manifests give repeatability, peer review and automated deployment.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: student-portal
  labels:
    app: student-portal
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: student-portal
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: student-portal
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/student-portal:1.4.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 256Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: student-portal
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: student-portal
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Read this example for four things:

  • Labels connect objects. selector.matchLabels must match the Pod template labels; that is how the Deployment and Service find their Pods.
  • Specific image tag (1.4.2), never latest, so every Pod runs the same code and rollback means something.
  • maxUnavailable: 0 means a rollout never reduces serving capacity.
  • ClusterIP is internal only. External access comes from an Ingress.

docs.title: Requests and limits
docs.text:
Setting Used by Effect Request Scheduler Decides which node has room. No request = Pod looks "free", nodes get overpacked Memory limit Runtime Exceeding it kills the container (OOMKilled) CPU limit Runtime Exceeding it throttles (slows) the container; no kill

Safe starting point: memory request = memory limit; a CPU request with no CPU limit for latency-sensitive services. Base values on observed usage.

docs.title: Probes
docs.text:
Probe Question On failure Readiness Can this Pod serve traffic now? Removed from the Service until it recovers Liveness Is the process stuck? Container restarted Startup Has a slow app finished starting? Liveness checks held off until it succeeds

Never make a liveness probe check the database

A short database outage would fail liveness on every replica at once, restarting them all and turning a blip into a full outage. Liveness tests only the process. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which removes the Pod from traffic instead of restarting it.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. A chart bundles templates with a values.yaml of defaults:

student-portal-chart/
├── Chart.yaml          # chart name and version
├── values.yaml         # default settings: the chart's public interface
└── templates/
    ├── deployment.yaml # templates with placeholders filled from values
    └── service.yaml

Templates contain placeholders (such as .Values.replicaCount) that Helm fills in. Each environment needs only a small values file:

# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 6
image:
  repository: 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/student-portal
  tag: "1.4.2"
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi

Every install or upgrade becomes a numbered release revision, which makes rollback possible:

# Install-or-upgrade in one idempotent command (the form used in pipelines)
helm upgrade --install portal ./student-portal-chart -f values-prod.yaml

# Inspect history and roll back to revision 2
helm history portal
helm rollback portal 2

# Render locally without touching the cluster, to review the output
helm template portal ./student-portal-chart -f values-prod.yaml

Most third-party software (monitoring stacks, the AWS Load Balancer Controller) is installed with Helm.

Common Helm pitfalls

Quote number-like values (tag: "1.10"), because unquoted 1.10 becomes 1.1. Use committed values files instead of --set, which leaves no record. Run helm template before upgrading to catch errors early.

Kustomize is the template-free alternative built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k): a shared base of plain YAML plus small per-environment patches.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text: Component Role in deployment eksctl / CloudFormation / CDK / Terraform Create the cluster, roles, network, node groups and add-ons kubeconfig Client config; gets short-lived tokens via aws eks get-token kubectl Inspect, diagnose and apply manifests Manifests Declarative YAML for application objects Helm chart, values, release Versioned, parameterised package with history and rollback Amazon ECR Stores the versioned images manifests reference CI/CD pipeline Builds, scans and pushes images, then applies manifests or Helm releases (Unit 5) Deployment controller Performs rolling updates inside the cluster metrics-server + HPA Scale replicas from metrics AWS Load Balancer Controller Turns Ingress into an ALB

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning eksctl CLI that creates EKS clusters and supporting AWS resources ClusterConfig Declarative YAML file read by eksctl kubeconfig / context Client config file / one cluster-plus-identity entry in it Manifest YAML file describing Kubernetes objects Deployment Maintains replicas of a Pod template and performs rolling updates ReplicaSet Per-version object a Deployment creates; rollout undo switches between them maxSurge / maxUnavailable Extra Pods allowed / missing Pods allowed during a rollout progressDeadlineSeconds Time before a stalled rollout is marked failed (no rollback) Requests / limits Scheduling amount / runtime ceiling Readiness / liveness / startup probe Can it serve / is it stuck / has it started Helm chart Versioned package of templates, values and metadata Release Named installation of a chart, with revision history Kustomize Base + overlay customisation built into kubectl ImagePullBackOff Node cannot pull the image: wrong name, tag or permissions CrashLoopBackOff Container keeps starting and exiting; check kubectl logs --previous OOMKilled Container exceeded its memory limit

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Cluster-level settings are in 3.1; node groups and add-ons in 3.3.

Setting Options Recommendation strategy.type RollingUpdate, Recreate Rolling for anything serving traffic; Recreate only if two versions must never coexist maxSurge / maxUnavailable Counts or percentages maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 for services that must not lose capacity replicas Integer At least 2 (ideally 3) for anything important Packaging tool Plain YAML, Kustomize, Helm YAML for small apps; Helm for third-party or heavily parameterised apps Image reference Mutable tag, unique tag, digest Unique immutable tag or digest; never latest Values management Committed files or --set Committed files Secrets Kubernetes Secret, or Secrets Manager via driver Secrets Manager; never plaintext in Git

docs.title: Design Considerations
docs.text: Quality Meaning Design levers Trade-off Reproducibility Cluster and apps can be rebuilt from code IaC, manifests in Git, versioned images Every change needs a commit Safety of change A bad release does not reach every user Readiness probes, maxUnavailable: 0, rollout status Slower rollouts Recoverability Rollback is fast and trustworthy Immutable tags, rollout undo, helm rollback Image versioning discipline

docs.title: Manifests versus Helm
docs.text:
Characteristic Plain manifests Helm charts Purpose Describe resources Package and parameterise applications Environment variation Separate files or Kustomize overlays One chart, per-environment values Rollback Deployment revisions Built-in release revisions Learning curve Lower Higher

Use plain manifests for simple apps with few environments. Use Helm for reusable apps, many variations, or third-party software. Do not adopt Helm just because it exists.

docs.title: AWS Best Practices
docs.text: Pillar Practice Operational Excellence Cluster as code, workloads as manifests in Git; kubectl rollout status in every pipeline; rehearse upgrades in non-production Security Least-privilege pipeline access; no secrets in images or Git; scan images Reliability Multiple replicas across AZs; correct readiness and liveness probes; maxUnavailable: 0 Performance Efficiency Small images; requests from observed usage; no CPU limits on latency-sensitive services Cost Optimization Right-size requests (they drive node count); share clusters with namespaces; delete unused clusters and load balancers Sustainability Accurate requests and switching off idle non-production environments

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Performance. Rollout time ≈ number of batches × (image pull + start + readiness). Small images and a startupProbe for slow apps keep it short. A readiness probe that passes too early sends traffic to Pods that cannot serve it. Preview changes with helm template or kubectl diff -f.

Cost. Requests drive node count, so over-requesting silently inflates the bill. Scale non-production down when unused.

Deleting a Deployment does not delete everything

Load balancers (from Services or Ingresses) and EBS volumes (from persistent volume claims) are AWS resources that can outlive the Kubernetes objects or even the cluster. Delete Services, Ingresses and PVCs before deleting the cluster, then check the console.

Monitoring.

Signal Source Tells you Rollout result kubectl rollout status Did the deployment actually finish? Pod events kubectl describe pod Plain-language cause of start-up failures Restarts and OOMKilled kubectl get pods, Container Insights Crash loops; memory limits too low CPU and memory usage kubectl top pods, Container Insights Actual usage vs requests ALB 5xx and unhealthy targets CloudWatch User-facing view of a bad rollout Control plane audit log CloudWatch Logs Who applied what, and when

Useful alarms: a Deployment that stops progressing, sustained Pod restarts, rising ALB 5xx during a release. More in 7.1.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Declarative. Controllers keep the described state true, even after failures.
  • Manifest = executable documentation. Image, resources, probes and identity in one reviewable file.
  • Fast rollback. kubectl rollout undo and helm rollback, if images are immutable.
  • Zero-downtime updates. Rolling updates with readiness probes.
  • Reuse across environments. Values files or overlays express only the differences.
  • Portable skills. kubectl, manifests and Helm work on any conformant cluster.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No automatic rollback. Less safe out of the box than the ECS circuit breaker.
  • YAML is error-prone, and templated YAML more so.
  • Many tools to learn and secure: kubectl, eksctl, Helm, controllers, CI/CD.
  • kubectl apply reports acceptance, not success.
  • Secrets need extra components such as Secrets Manager plus a driver.
  • Multi-layer debugging. A failure may be the app, the image, a permission, scheduling or a probe.

docs.title: Beginner mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text: Mistake Reality Do instead "kubectl creates the EKS cluster" Cluster creation is an AWS operation Use eksctl, console or IaC "eksctl replaces kubectl" One builds the cluster, the other manages workloads Use both, each for its job "Helm is mandatory" Useful, not required Plain manifests for simple apps Treating kubectl apply as success It returns when stored, not running Follow with kubectl rollout status image: myapp:latest Pods may run different code; rollback meaningless Unique tag per build No resource requests Scheduler overpacks nodes Set requests from observed usage Liveness probe checks the database A DB blip restarts every replica Dependencies go in readiness Fixing things with kubectl edit Unreviewed and later overwritten Change the manifest, apply, commit Committing a Secret to Git Credential exposed in history forever Secrets Manager with a driver Copying YAML per environment Copies drift apart One chart or base, per-env values Running databases in Kubernetes by default More operational burden Prefer RDS or DynamoDB

docs.title: Production mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Remedy Pipeline with cluster-admin credentials One compromised build controls the cluster Scope pipeline access tightly Upgrading without checking removed APIs Workloads break after a one-way upgrade Scan manifests; upgrade non-production first Mixing eksctl and Terraform on one cluster Conflicting state, hidden stacks One provisioning tool per cluster --set in automation Real config hidden in a pipeline script Committed values files Assuming a stalled rollout recovers Stays failed rollout status + rollout undo in the pipeline Deleting the cluster before Services and volumes Orphaned load balancers and EBS keep billing Scripted teardown, then verify

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Deploying on EKS is a layered process:

  1. Package the app as an image with a unique version and push it to ECR.
  2. Provision the cluster and nodes with eksctl or IaC.
  3. Describe the app as Kubernetes objects (manifests or a Helm chart).
  4. Apply them, then confirm with kubectl rollout status.
  5. Expose it with a Service and an Ingress (ALB).
  6. Give it AWS access through workload identity, never stored keys.
  7. Monitor the whole application, not just the cluster.
Key lesson Why it matters Keep provisioning, packaging and delivery separate They change at different rates and carry different risks eksctl builds the cluster; kubectl and Helm run the apps Different tools, different jobs Requests schedule, memory limits kill, CPU limits throttle A few fields decide behaviour Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts Wrong probe design causes outages Kubernetes does not roll back for you Always check rollout status; be ready to undo Upgrade order: control plane → add-ons → nodes Nodes never run ahead of the control plane

Next: this topic treated "the nodes" as a given. 3.3 looks at the data plane options in depth: Fargate profiles, managed node groups and add-ons.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
3.1 showed that AWS runs the EKS control plane while you choose the data plane. 3.2 deployed applications onto "the nodes". This topic looks at the three EKS features that shape that data plane:

  • AWS Fargate on EKS runs selected Pods on serverless compute. Each Pod gets its own isolated micro-VM; there is no node to create, patch or size. A Fargate profile decides which Pods run this way.
  • EKS managed node groups are EC2 instances acting as nodes, where EKS automates the lifecycle: launching from an EKS-optimized AMI, joining the cluster, replacing unhealthy instances, and safe upgrades. You still choose instance types and scaling limits.
  • EKS add-ons are AWS-packaged, versioned installs of components every cluster needs (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy), managed through the EKS API instead of loose YAML.
Mechanism Removes from you Costs you Fargate profile The node: no AMI, patching or capacity planning No DaemonSets, EBS, GPUs or privileged containers; per-Pod pricing; slower start Managed node group AMI choice, bootstrap, registration, safe node replacement You still choose instance types, scaling and upgrade timing EKS add-on Building and version-matching core components A version to update with every cluster upgrade

These combine; they are not alternatives

A typical production cluster runs managed node groups for most workloads, Fargate for a few namespaces, and core add-ons managed by EKS. The real skill is explaining which workload belongs where, and why.

docs.title: Why This Service or Concept Exists
docs.text: Pods must run somewhere. Traditionally that is an EC2 node you patch, size, secure and pay for whether it is full or not. Different workloads tolerate that overhead differently.

docs.title: Why Fargate exists
docs.text:
Workload Why a node is a poor fit Small service needing 0.25 vCPU Smallest sensible node is much bigger and mostly idle CI job running four minutes Launching and draining a node takes longer than the job Untrusted or customer code Pods on a shared node share one kernel, a weaker boundary than a VM Bursty, unpredictable traffic Capacity must be guessed in advance

Fargate makes the Pod itself the unit of compute: AWS creates a micro-VM sized to the Pod and bills per second. Almost every Fargate limitation follows from this one decision, so understand the reason rather than memorising the list.

docs.title: Why managed node groups exist
docs.text: Self-managed nodes mean choosing an AMI, writing bootstrap scripts, building an Auto Scaling group, registering nodes, replacing failures and, hardest of all, upgrading without dropping traffic. This work is easy to get subtly wrong. Managed node groups do it behind one API and leave you the decisions that are really about the workload.

docs.title: Why add-ons exist
docs.text: The network plugin, DNS and Service proxy are separate open-source projects with their own release cycles. Installed as loose kubectl apply files, nobody knows which version runs, nobody updates them, and a later cluster upgrade fails mysteriously. EKS add-ons give each one a version, configuration and update operation, visible in the EKS API and CloudTrail.

docs.title: The compute-management spectrum
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    SELF["Self-managed EC2 nodes"] --> MNG["EKS managed node groups"]
    MNG --> FARGATE["EKS on AWS Fargate"]
    FARGATE --> HIGH["Higher abstraction"]

Moving right: fewer servers to manage, less low-level control, more workload constraints, and pricing shifts from per instance to per Pod. Neither end is universally better.

Model Who manages the node You still decide Self-managed You: AMI, bootstrap, registration, upgrades Everything Managed node group EKS automates provisioning, replacement, updates Instance types, scaling limits, labels, taints, upgrade timing Fargate AWS; no node is visible to you Pod resource requests and which Pods use Fargate

docs.title: Key ideas
docs.text:
• Fargate changes where Pods run, not how Kubernetes works. Deployments, Services, RBAC and the API are unchanged.
  • A managed node group is still EC2, in your account, billed as normal EC2.
  • Add-ons are data plane software. They run as Pods and must match the control plane version.
  • One cluster can mix models, placing each workload where its trade-offs fit.

docs.title: EKS Fargate profiles
docs.text:
What a profile contains. A name, a Pod execution role, a list of private subnets, and up to five selectors. Each selector needs a namespace and may add labels.

fargateProfiles:
  - name: ci-runners
    podExecutionRoleARN: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/EksFargatePodExecutionRole
    subnets: [subnet-0a1, subnet-0b1, subnet-0c1]   # private subnets only
    selectors:
      - namespace: ci
        labels:
          runner: "true"        # namespace AND label must both match
      - namespace: preview-*    # wildcards are supported

Here, Pods in ci labelled runner: "true" run on Fargate, as do all Pods in any preview-* namespace. Everything else runs on EC2 nodes.

Rule Meaning Namespace is required Labels alone cannot select a Pod Labels within a selector: AND All must match Selectors within a profile: OR Any one may match Wildcards * and ? allowed Profiles are immutable To change, create a new profile and delete the old Deleting a profile stops its Pods They become Pending Private subnets only No public IP; egress via NAT gateway or VPC endpoints

How a Pod reaches Fargate:

flowchart TD
    POD["Pod created in namespace 'ci', labelled runner=true"] --> MATCH{"Matches a Fargate profile selector?"}
    MATCH -->|"No"| NODE["Scheduled onto an EC2 node as normal"]
    MATCH -->|"Yes"| FSCHED["Assigned to the Fargate scheduler"]
    FSCHED --> PROV["AWS provisions a micro-VM sized to the Pod's requests"]
    PROV --> ENI["Pod gets a VPC IP in one of the profile's private subnets"]
    ENI --> PULL["Image pulled using the Pod execution role"]
    PULL --> RUN["Pod runs; shows as its own fargate- node in kubectl get nodes"]
    RUN --> DONE["Pod ends; micro-VM destroyed, nothing reused"]

Because nothing is reused (no warm capacity, no image cache), Fargate Pods start more slowly than Pods on an existing node.

Design selectors around stable namespaces

Profiles cannot be edited, and deleting one stops its Pods. Select on stable namespaces like ci or tenant-plugins, not labels teams change often.

Fargate limitations, and why they exist:

Limitation Reason No DaemonSets A DaemonSet runs one Pod per node; there is no shared node No privileged containers They could reach the host, which AWS owns No hostNetwork / hostPort No customer host network to join No GPUs Capacity is standard AWS compute, not a chosen instance type No EBS volumes EBS attaches to an instance; use EFS instead No EKS Pod Identity Its agent is a DaemonSet; use IRSA (3.1) Load balancer targets must use IP mode There is no instance to register Slower Pod start New micro-VM plus uncached image pull

Billing. Per second (one-minute minimum) for the vCPU and memory the Pod requests, rounded up to the nearest supported size. Fargate adds about 256 MB per Pod for Kubernetes components. Sizes range from 0.25 vCPU / 0.5 GB to 16 vCPU / 120 GB. Each Pod gets 20 GiB ephemeral storage by default.

Requested (all containers) Allocated and billed 0.4 vCPU, 1.5 GB 0.5 vCPU, 2 GB 1 vCPU, 7.5 GB 1 vCPU, 8 GB 3 vCPU, 5 GB 4 vCPU, 8 GB

On Fargate, requests are the bill

On EC2 nodes, an oversized request mainly affects how many Pods fit. On Fargate, the rounded-up request is exactly what you pay.

Other Fargate details:

  • Pod execution role: used by AWS to register the Pod and pull images. Application containers cannot use it; give them IRSA.
  • Storage: ephemeral storage dies with the Pod. Persistent or shared storage = EFS CSI driver.
  • Logging: no node for a logging DaemonSet, so use the built-in Fluent Bit router, configured with a ConfigMap in the aws-observability namespace.

docs.title: EKS managed node groups
docs.text:
What it is. EKS creates an EC2 Auto Scaling group and launch template in your account and operates them as Kubernetes nodes. No extra charge beyond EC2.

flowchart TB
    EKS["EKS control plane"] --> MNG["Managed node group: instance types, sizes, labels, taints"]
    MNG --> ASG["EC2 Auto Scaling group (created by EKS)"]
    ASG --> EC2A["EC2 node - AZ A"]
    ASG --> EC2B["EC2 node - AZ B"]
    ASG --> EC2C["EC2 node - AZ C"]
    EC2A --> P1["Pods"]
    EC2B --> P2["Pods"]
    EC2C --> P3["Pods"]
Self-managed burden Managed node group provides Choose and track an AMI AWS-published EKS-optimized AMIs per Kubernetes version Bootstrap scripts Automatic Let nodes join the cluster Access entry for the node role created automatically Replace unhealthy nodes Health monitoring and automatic replacement Upgrade safely Rolling replacement with cordon and drain Spot interruptions Nodes drained when AWS signals reclamation

AMI families.

AMI Use Amazon Linux 2023 General-purpose default Bottlerocket Minimal container OS: read-only root, no shell; smaller attack surface, faster boot, harder to customise GPU AMIs Include drivers for machine learning Windows Windows containers

How node updates work. Nodes are replaced, not upgraded in place:

  1. Launch new nodes with the new AMI.
  2. Cordon an old node: no new Pods scheduled there.
  3. Drain it: evict its Pods so their controllers recreate them elsewhere, respecting each workload's PodDisruptionBudget (PDB).
  4. Terminate the old node and repeat.

updateConfig sets how many nodes are replaced at once (maxUnavailable count or maxUnavailablePercentage). Small = safer; large = faster.

A PodDisruptionBudget can block an upgrade

A PDB limits how many Pods of an app may be evicted at once, keeping it available during drains. But if it allows zero disruptions (for example minAvailable: 3 with three replicas), the drain never completes and the update times out. Keep minAvailable below the replica count or use maxUnavailable: 1. Check kubectl get pdb -A and the ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column before upgrading. The force option ignores PDBs: an emergency escape, not a fix.

Spot capacity. SPOT capacity type uses spare EC2 capacity at a large discount, but AWS can reclaim it with a two-minute warning. Managed node groups drain the affected node automatically. To use Spot well:

  • specify several compatible instance types, so one reclaimed pool does not remove the group;
  • run only interruption-tolerant work (batch, CI, stateless workers);
  • keep an On-Demand group that can carry essential traffic alone, with Spot above it (the same base-plus-Spot idea as ECS capacity providers in 2.3).

Availability Zones. Span node groups across AZs. But a multi-AZ node group alone is not high availability: the app also needs replicas spread across zones, and resilient dependencies.

Names to know.

  • Karpenter: open-source autoscaler that launches right-sized EC2 instances directly for pending Pods, instead of scaling a fixed group.
  • EKS Auto Mode: AWS runs the whole data plane for an extra fee.
  • Launch template: customises disk size, security groups and instance metadata (for example IMDSv2 hop limit 1, see 3.1). A custom AMI in it means EKS no longer updates that image for you.

docs.title: EKS add-ons
docs.text:
What it is. An AWS-managed install of a cluster component with a name, version, optional configuration, and optionally its own IAM role. No extra charge beyond resources used.

The core networking add-ons were explained in 3.1. Here the focus is what breaks without each one:

Add-on Job Symptom when missing or broken Amazon VPC CNI VPC IPs for Pods Nodes never Ready; Pods stuck ContainerCreating CoreDNS Service name resolution Scattered timeouts that look like unrelated errors kube-proxy Service virtual IP routing ClusterIP Services unreachable from affected nodes Amazon EBS CSI driver Creates and attaches EBS volumes for PVCs PVCs stay Pending; stateful apps never start EKS Pod Identity Agent Per-Pod IAM credentials Pods cannot get their AWS permissions

Other add-ons: the EFS CSI driver (shared storage; the persistent option for Fargate) and the CloudWatch Observability agent (Container Insights).

CoreDNS failures look like everything failing

DNS problems rarely say "DNS is down". Run CoreDNS with at least two replicas across nodes and zones, and monitor its errors and latency.

Add-ons and upgrades. Add-ons must match the control plane version. Update them as the middle step of every upgrade: control plane → add-ons → nodes (3.2). Pin versions in IaC.

Give add-ons their own IAM role. The EBS CSI driver creates volumes; the VPC CNI manages ENIs. Putting these permissions on the node role hands them to every Pod on the node.

Operators, briefly. An operator is a custom resource type plus a controller that keeps the real world matching it. The AWS Load Balancer Controller (Ingress → ALB) is a familiar example.

docs.title: Fargate versus managed node groups
docs.text: Dimension Fargate Managed node groups Compute AWS micro-VM per Pod EC2 instances in your account Node administration None Reduced; upgrades and sizing remain Instance type / GPUs No Yes DaemonSets No Yes EBS volumes No (EFS only) Yes Workload identity IRSA only Pod Identity or IRSA Density One Pod per micro-VM Many Pods per node Isolation Per-Pod VM Shared node kernel Pod start Slower Fast when capacity exists Pricing Per Pod, by requested vCPU and memory Per instance, full or not Best fit Small, bursty, short-lived, untrusted Steady, dense, specialised, node-dependent

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Fargate profile Selects which Pods run on Fargate, and in which private subnets Pod execution role IAM role AWS uses to start Fargate Pods and pull images Fargate micro-VM Isolated compute for one Pod, destroyed when it ends Fargate log router Built-in Fluent Bit, configured in aws-observability Managed node group EKS-operated EC2 nodes with lifecycle automation Auto Scaling group + launch template Created by EKS to launch and replace nodes EKS-optimized AMI Node image with kubelet, containerd and bootstrap tooling PodDisruptionBudget Limits evictions per workload during drains EKS add-ons Versioned core components (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, CSI drivers, Pod Identity Agent)

Three groups: compute (Fargate, node groups: where Pods run), platform components (add-ons: needed by every cluster), and the supporting AWS services from 3.1.

docs.title: Important AWS Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning AWS Fargate Serverless compute; one micro-VM per Pod Fargate profile Selects which Pods run on Fargate, and where Selector Required namespace plus optional labels; up to five per profile Pod execution role IAM role AWS uses to run Fargate Pods Managed node group EKS-operated Auto Scaling group of EC2 nodes Self-managed node EC2 instance you bootstrap, register and upgrade EKS-optimized AMI AWS-published node image for a Kubernetes version Bottlerocket Minimal, immutable container-focused OS Launch template Customises node disks, security groups, metadata options Cordon / drain Stop new Pods on a node / evict its Pods PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) Limits voluntary evictions for a workload updateConfig How many nodes are replaced at once Capacity type On-Demand, Spot or Capacity Blocks Spot interruption notice Two-minute warning before Spot reclamation Karpenter Autoscaler launching right-sized nodes for pending Pods EKS add-on AWS-managed, versioned cluster component CSI driver Plugin connecting Kubernetes to EBS or EFS storage Operator Custom resource + controller automating a system

docs.title: Fargate
docs.text: Setting Options Recommendation Selectors Namespace + optional labels Namespace-only, on stable namespaces Subnets Private only Several AZs Pod execution role IAM role Image pull and registration only Workload identity IRSA Pod Identity not supported Resource requests vCPU, memory Accurate: rounded up and billed Persistent storage EFS EBS not supported Logging Fluent Bit ConfigMap Configure at cluster build

docs.title: Managed node groups
docs.text: Setting Options Recommendation AMI type AL2023, Bottlerocket, GPU, Windows AL2023 or Bottlerocket Instance types One or several Several, especially for Spot Capacity type On-Demand, Spot, Capacity Blocks On-Demand base; Spot for tolerant work Scaling minSize, maxSize, desiredSize Min covers baseline; max caps cost Subnets One or more Two, preferably three, AZs Labels and taints Any Labels guide placement; taints reserve nodes updateConfig Count or percentage Small for small groups; about 25% for large Launch template Optional Disk size, security groups, IMDS settings

docs.title: Add-ons
docs.text: Setting Options Recommendation Which add-ons Core + optional VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, Pod Identity Agent; EBS CSI if stateful Version Explicit or default Pin in IaC Configuration JSON/YAML via EKS API Keep in code (for example CoreDNS replicas) IAM role IRSA or Pod Identity Own role per add-on, not the node role

docs.title: Decision framework
docs.text:
Ask these for each workload:

  1. Needs node-level features? GPUs, DaemonSets, EBS, privileged mode, host networking → managed node group.
  2. Untrusted or multi-tenant code? → Fargate's per-Pod VM boundary.
  3. Usage pattern? Bursty, short-lived or tiny → Fargate (no idle node). Steady and dense → well-packed nodes are cheaper.
  4. Fast scale-out on the user path? Nodes with spare capacity respond faster than new Fargate micro-VMs.
  5. Full cost? Include utilisation, idle capacity, operations effort, storage and logs, not just unit price.
flowchart TD
    A["A workload arrives. Where should it run?"] --> B{"Needs GPU, DaemonSet, EBS, privileged mode, or host networking?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["Managed node group"]
    B -->|"No"| D{"Untrusted or multi-tenant code?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Fargate profile"]
    D -->|"No"| F{"Bursty, short-lived, or very small?"}
    F -->|"Yes"| E
    F -->|"No: steady and dense"| C
    C --> G{"Tolerates interruption?"}
    G -->|"Yes"| H["Spot node group above an On-Demand base"]
    G -->|"No"| I["On-Demand node group"]

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Core trade-off

More abstraction reduces infrastructure management, but also reduces low-level control.

Quality Fargate Managed node groups Operational burden Lowest Moderate Isolation Per-Pod VM Shared node kernel Cost, steady workloads Higher Lower when well packed Cost, bursty workloads Lower (no idle nodes) Higher if nodes sit idle Elasticity Per Pod, slower start Fast with headroom Flexibility Constrained High

docs.title: Architecture scenarios
docs.text:
Scenario 1: small internal APIs. Moderate, unpredictable traffic; team wants minimal admin. Fargate fits if the services meet its constraints: no nodes, pay per running Pod.

Scenario 2: high-throughput service. Needs predictable compute, high density, specific instance families and node monitoring agents. Managed node groups fit.

Scenario 3: mixed. One cluster, both models:

flowchart TB
    EKS["EKS cluster"]
    EKS --> F["Fargate profiles"]
    EKS --> M["Managed node groups"]
    F --> API["Small internal APIs"]
    F --> JOB["Short-lived CI and batch jobs"]
    F --> UNTRUSTED["Untrusted plugin code"]
    M --> WEB["High-throughput services"]
    M --> GPU["GPU workloads"]
    M --> AGENT["Workloads needing DaemonSets or EBS"]

Principle: choose the compute model per workload, not one model for everything.

docs.title: AWS Best Practices
docs.text: Pillar Practice Operational Excellence Node groups, Fargate profiles and add-ons in IaC with pinned versions; update add-ons in every upgrade Security Fargate for untrusted code; own IAM role per add-on; minimal node role; Bottlerocket where suitable Reliability Node groups across AZs; CoreDNS with 2+ replicas; PDBs that allow at least one disruption Performance Efficiency Match compute model to workload shape; small images (especially on Fargate); keep node headroom Cost Optimization Spot above an On-Demand base; Fargate where nodes would idle; Graviton where images support ARM Sustainability Dense packing; scale batch node groups to zero when idle

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Fargate isolation is a real boundary. A container escape on a shared node reaches a kernel shared with other Pods; on Fargate it reaches an AWS kernel running one Pod. Apply it to just the namespaces that need it.
  • No node role on Fargate to misuse. The Pod execution role is not available to containers. On EC2 nodes, block IMDS with hop limit 1 (3.1).
  • Add-ons get their own roles, not the node role.
  • Harden nodes. Encrypted EBS, Systems Manager instead of SSH, minimal AMI, regular updates.
  • Private subnets for Fargate Pods and nodes; NAT or VPC endpoints for egress.

Review what you install

Helm charts and add-ons often create cluster-wide permissions. Read what they create, and install only what the cluster needs.

docs.title: Operating It: Performance, Cost and Monitoring
docs.text:
Performance. A latency-sensitive service that must scale out fast is better on nodes with spare capacity than on Fargate. Keep images small, scale CoreDNS with the cluster, keep node headroom.

Cost.

Lever Helps by Caution Spot above On-Demand base Big discount Must tolerate rescheduling; use several types Fargate for bursty work No idle nodes Costlier for steady work Accurate requests Fewer nodes / smaller Fargate bill Too low hurts performance Graviton (ARM) Better price-performance Needs ARM images Scale batch groups to zero No idle cost Only for work that really stops

Fargate is not always cheaper

Cost depends on utilisation, requests and density. Compare per workload.

Monitoring.

Signal Source Tells you Pending Pods kubectl get pods, events No matching capacity or Fargate profile Node group update status aws eks describe-nodegroup Upgrade progressing or stuck PDBs kubectl get pdb -A ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0 will block drains Fargate Pods kubectl get nodes -l eks.amazonaws.com/compute-type=fargate What runs (and bills) on Fargate Add-on health and version aws eks describe-addon Version drift or degraded add-on CoreDNS errors and latency Container Insights DNS trouble before it spreads Audit trail CloudTrail Who changed node groups, profiles, add-ons

Running is not healthy

A Running Pod can still return errors. Monitor latency and error rates too.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Compute is a per-workload choice. Fargate and node groups coexist in one cluster.
  • Fargate removes node management and gives per-Pod isolation.
  • Managed node groups keep control without the plumbing. AMIs, bootstrap, replacement and rolling updates handled.
  • Spot becomes practical through automatic draining.
  • Add-ons are visible and upgradable through the EKS API.
  • No extra management charge for node groups or AWS add-ons.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Fargate's limits are structural (no node): no DaemonSets, privileged containers, GPUs, EBS or Pod Identity; slower start.
  • Fargate is costly for steady, dense work.
  • Fargate profiles are immutable.
  • Node groups do not pick sizes for you; varied needs may need several groups.
  • Your own PDBs can block node updates.
  • Custom AMIs shift update responsibility back to you.
  • Add-ons need updating with every Kubernetes upgrade.

docs.title: Beginner mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text: Mistake Why it is wrong Do instead "Fargate is always cheaper" Steady workloads are often cheaper on nodes Compare full cost per workload "Fargate eliminates Kubernetes" Only the compute layer changes Manage Deployments, Services, RBAC as normal "Managed node groups = managing each instance by hand" EKS automates lifecycle Focus on sizing and scaling "One compute model per cluster" Models coexist Choose per workload Whole cluster on Fargate Loses DaemonSets, EBS, GPUs; costs more for steady work Fargate for specific namespaces Expecting DaemonSets or EBS on Fargate No node to run on or attach to Fluent Bit, sidecars, EFS, or nodes Pod Identity on Fargate Agent is a DaemonSet IRSA Editing a Fargate profile Immutable Create new, delete old One instance type for Spot One reclaimed pool removes the group Several compatible types

docs.title: Production mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Remedy PDB allowing zero disruptions Node upgrades stall and time out Allow at least one; check before upgrades Routinely forcing node updates PDBs give no protection Fix the budgets instead Add-ons skipped during upgrades Networking or DNS failures Update between control plane and nodes CoreDNS with one replica Cluster-wide mysterious timeouts 2+ replicas across zones Add-ons using the node role Every Pod gains their permissions Own role per add-on All Spot, no On-Demand base One capacity event removes the workload On-Demand base + diverse Spot All nodes in one AZ One zone failure = no capacity Span multiple AZs No Fargate log routing Fargate logs lost Configure aws-observability at build

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
EKS compute is a trade-off between control, operational effort, flexibility, density and cost.

Feature Key lesson Data plane choice Per workload. Fargate and node groups can share a cluster; start from workload requirements Fargate For small, bursty, short-lived or untrusted Pods. Limits (no DaemonSets, EBS, GPUs, Pod Identity; billed on rounded-up requests) all follow from "no node" Fargate profiles Namespace + optional labels; immutable; design around stable namespaces Managed node groups For EC2-level control, special hardware, node agents, density. EKS handles AMIs, replacement and rolling updates PDBs Protect availability during drains, but zero slack blocks upgrades Spot Several instance types, tolerant workloads, On-Demand base Add-ons Essential data plane software; pin versions, own IAM roles, update every upgrade

Unit 3 in one line: 3.1 built the cluster, 3.2 deployed onto it, 3.3 chose the right compute underneath each workload.

Practice and interview questions

Questions for this topic are kept separately: Practice questions · Interview questions.

docs.title: Unit 4: Microservice Architecture
docs.text:
Learning Outcome

Architect microservices-based applications on AWS, utilizing services such as API Gateway, AppSync, and App Mesh for effective service communication and management.

Apply AWS-specific patterns and best practices for building resilient, scalable, and high-performance cloud-native applications.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text: Topic Title 4.1 Microservices Design Principles 4.2 API Management and Service Mesh 4.3 Resilience in AWS Microservices

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
• Unit 4 Practice Questions
  • Unit 4 Interview Questions

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Microservices design principles are the set of rules an architect applies when converting a business domain into a collection of independently deployable services on a cloud platform. On AWS, the principles are the same as anywhere else; what changes is that AWS supplies a specific, opinionated toolkit for each of them, and that the choice of tool has direct consequences for cost, latency, operational load, and how difficult a boundary is to move later.

Three principles dominate, and this chapter is organised around them.

Principle The question it answers The failure it prevents Primary AWS instruments Decomposition by business capability Where does one service end and the next begin? Boundaries drawn on technical layers, producing a distributed monolith Domain analysis, AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces, Application Discovery Service, App2Container Explicit, versioned contracts over the network How do services talk, and who owns the contract? Implicit coupling through shared libraries, shared schemas, or undocumented behaviour Amazon API Gateway, AWS AppSync (including Merged APIs), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon VPC Lattice Exclusive data ownership Who is allowed to write this row, and who may only ask? A shared database that re-couples services while keeping the network hops Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Aurora and Aurora DSQL, Amazon RDS, Amazon DocumentDB, Amazon Neptune, Amazon Keyspaces, Amazon MemoryDB, Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon Timestream, Amazon OpenSearch Service

A fourth principle design for failure is equally definitional but is treated separately in chapter 4.3, because on AWS it has its own distinct toolkit.

Within an AWS architecture these principles operate at three different layers. Decomposition is an analysis-time activity that produces no AWS resources at all; it produces a boundary map. Communication is an edge and east-west concern realised in API Gateway, AppSync, ALB, VPC Lattice, EventBridge, SQS and SNS. Data ownership is a persistence-tier concern realised in the choice and configuration of purpose-built databases and in the pipelines that move data between them without granting one service write access to another's tables.
